speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege concerning this house and all hon. members in it. My question of privilege involves an answer given yesterday to a question of mine, and may I preface it by pointing out that in Hansard for June 7, 1961, at page 5965, certain information was given in reply to a question by the hon. member for St. Denis indicating travelling expenses of the Postmaster General for the month of May to the extent of $317.33, and indicating that certain other transportation was provided for the Postmaster General free of charge by government services.
Yesterday the question I asked, and which was answered, was as follows:
Did any members of the cabinet incur any travelling expenses between April 1, 1962, and June 30, 1962, inclusive?
To this the answer was yes. The second part of my question read:
If so, for each member of cabinet, what was, for each day, the amount of expenses incurred, the point or place travelled to, and the purpose of the visit?
The answer to this was:
The information available does not permit an answer to be given to this part of the question.
I submit, by virtue of the fact that a somewhat similar question was answered in 1961, this information is available, and my question of privilege is that the government is withholding information from parliament relating to travelling expenses of cabinet ministers and accordingly should be censured for it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement in regard to the Cuban situation. I do not intend to recapitulate the events of the last few days, all of which are known to hon. members. However, I think I should refer to President Kennedy's statement on Monday night that Russian action in placing missiles and bombers in Cuba threatens this continent and Central and South America. Indeed, the Soviet union by its action has reached out across the Atlantic to challenge the right of free men to live in peace in this hemisphere.
I think Canadians are in general agreement that these offensive weapons, located so contiguously to our continent are a direct and immediate menace to Canada. Furthermore, they are a serious menace to the deterrent strategic strength of the whole western alliance on which our security is founded. The result is that a threat is posed not only to this continent but to the NATO alliance as a whole, and indeed to all the free world, whose security depends to such an extent upon the strategic strength of the United States.
The United States government, as I have said on an earlier occasion, informed us of the facts of the situation and of the course of action proposed to be taken some few hours before President Kennedy made his announcement.

Crisis in Cuba
The government commenced immediately to consider the measures that the Canadian government and Canadian forces should take in order to be ready to deal with whatever eventualities would arise from this action. So that the attitude of the government will be clearly understood-and again I am asking for the support of the house as a whole in this connection-we intend to support the United States and our other allies in this situation.
It is a serious one. It has been necessary and will always remain necessary to weigh the risks both of action and inaction in such circumstances. I need not refer to the record of Canada in two world wars, in the NATO alliance and in Korea as demonstrating the fact that Canadians stand by their allies and their undertakings, and we intend in the present crisis to do the same. On the other hand, we shall not fail to do everything possible to seek solutions to these problems without war. We shall seek to avoid provocative action. Our purpose will be to do everything to reduce tension.
I think I should summarize some of the principal actions which have been taken by the government to date to deal with the question. The first, which was referred to by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, was to exercise a control over Soviet bloc aircraft bound for Cuba. He has explained these measures to the house in some detail; I would add simply that commencing even before the president's speech we had acted to ensure that Canadian air space and Canadian air transport facilities were not being used to carry arms to the Soviet bases in Cuba.
Second, all Canadian military forces have taken necessary precautionary measures to improve their readiness to meet any serious developments. The Canadian component of the NORAD forces has been placed upon the same level of readiness as the United States forces under NORAD operational control. Furthermore, as was stated by the Minister of National Defence, we have deferred any further movement of dependants of armed services personnel overseas. We have held up the authorization of any long leave for armed services personnel. The government today approved the measures which the forces would have to take in the event that the present crisis led to a more serious situation. Our civilian departments have been instructed as a matter of urgency to bring up to date the measures which they would need to take in any emergency. They are doing so. The ministers and key civilian officials have been asked to remain available during this period of crisis.

On other occasions I have informed the house of preparations for carrying on government should the worst occur. These preparations cover not only the public service but also provincial governments and municipalities which we have been financing and assisting with information and advice. I do not think I should go any further into detail in dealing with the measures which we have taken or would be prepared to take should circumstances require us to do so.
I wish the house and the Canadian people to know that the government has taken such precautions as are necessary at this stage to co-operate with our allies, and to be prepared for contingencies that might arise. As I said a moment ago, the government is seeking to find means by which the dangerous, threatening situation can be settled without recourse to arms. On the other hand, we recognize the fact that the free world as a whole cannot afford to permit its essential security to be endangered by offensive weapons mounted on bases adjacent to North America. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs said last evening during the course of his interview on the television facilities of the nation, we shall continue to do everything we can to avert the dangers to which we are exposed.
As far as the last twenty four hours are concerned, the main facts are well known to members of the house. Some Soviet ships have altered course away from Cuba. One Soviet tanker, after having been intercepted by a United States naval ship, was allowed to proceed on its way since it had been satisfactorily established that the cargo was petroleum.
I think we may take encouragement from the restraint being exercised at the moment. However, it would be dangerously premature to assume that the critical phase of the current situation has passed. There are two pressing needs to be met, namely not only to avoid conflict but to find a peaceful solution to this new Soviet challenge.
I think members of the house are in agreement that the greatest hope of finding such a solution lies in the United Nations. The acting secretary general is to be commended for the speed with which he has acted to discharge the heavy responsibility he bears as the executive head of the U.N. His proposal for a standstill is designed to gain the time that is so urgently needed while the search goes forward for some formula which will provide an acceptable solution. His offer of his personal good offices is in the best tradition of his predecessors in that office.

Meanwhile the security council is to meet again at four o'clock. There the formal discussions will be resumed. Perhaps by that time the replies of President Kennedy and Chairman Khrushchev will have been received.
There is a debate going on throughout the world regarding the legality of the quarantine measures which the United States has imposed. To my mind such arguments are largely sterile and irrelevant. We have a situation to face. Legalistic arguments, whatever they may be, cannot erase the fact that the Soviet union has posed a new and immediate threat to the security not only of the United States but of Canada as well.
Chairman Khrushchev's apologists say "What is the difference between Soviet missile bases in Cuba and United States bases on the periphery of the Soviet union?" The United States bases abroad have been installed only in response to the threatening pressures from the Soviet union, and have never been concealed from the public. The west, moreover, has refrained in recent years from any move to upset the world balance. There are countries in all parts of the world in which nuclear weapons could have been installed by the west. A deliberate decision was made not to do so. We in Canada have shown responsibility in this connection in order to avoid the proliferation of these dangerous weapons throughout the world. Sir, to compare the western activities with the provocative, clandestine arming of Cuba is to ignore the calculated restraint which has characterized western policy. In this light the call for the dismantling of these new, threatening facilities in Cuba is not unreasonable. It is the Soviet union itself which has disturbed the balance, and it is for it and Cuba to restore that balance.
The fact that we find ourselves in this dire situation may well have some salutary effect. Surely it is not too much to hope that some good will come out of the present dangerous situation. If these facilities were dismantled this would represent a first practical step on the road to disarmament, and if some such suggestion as I made a few days ago were coupled with international inspection of the process then we might well find ourselves taking the first steps away from the dangerous abyss that we have faced for so long in the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all members of the house will have welcomed the statement made by the Prime Minister in informing the house of developments in this very serious situation. It is not an exaggeration to say that it is more than serious, it is grave. While
Crisis in Cuba
the gravity of the situation has certainly not increased in the last 24 hours, nevertheless the threat to peace remains and will remain until we can be satisfied that steps have been taken to remove the threat with which we are now confronted.
That threat, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, is in the extension of nuclear bases from those countries which now, unfortunately, have them to a country which has not had such a base, a country which this time happens to be in the western hemisphere. This constitutes an immediate threat to the peace and security of the hemisphere, especially in view of the circumstances under which these bases in Cuba are being constructed.
This extension, Mr. Speaker, has important implications going beyond this immediate emergency, implications which are important in the formulation of our own policy for defence, and implications which underline the importance of all countries, which do not now possess nuclear weapons doing what they can to prevent their extension. Perhaps this can be done by these countries at the United Nations agreeing on a self denying ordinance to prevent such extension. However, there is no chance as I see it, of lessening tension generally in respect of this and related matters, easing tensions in the cold war itself, until we can remove this immediate threat to peace which has been provided by the extension of nuclear bases to Cuba.
The vital question, therefore, as has been pointed out by the Prime Minister is, are these bases being constructed? Are they a threat to security and peace? Are they under Soviet control? I think the evidence shows, without any possibility of doubt, that the answer to all these questions must be in the affirmative.
This is a new development and it is a new danger. It is a danger of which the President of the United States warned us on September 4 and again on September 13, when he said, on September 4, that there was no evidence of Soviet military bases in Cuba or the presence of offensive ground to ground missiles. Then, and perhaps we did not attach as much importance to these words at the time as we should have, he went on to say "were it otherwise the gravest issues would arise". Well, Mr. Speaker, they have arisen. So the President of the United States felt compelled to act in the interests of the security of his own country, and indeed the security of the hemisphere.
As I have already ventured to say we who are the closest neighbour and in some ways the closest friend of the United States, at this time of grave emergency and threat to peace

Crisis in Cuba
must support that action. But as I have already stated outside the house, we can, while supporting that action which is considered necessary in the interests of security in the face of this threat, be very grateful indeed that the United Nations has been called into session at this time and that the security council is already meeting. We can be grateful that at the United Nations, our world organization, they are working, talking and negotiating to solve this problem in a way which will remove it as a threat to peace.
I think we can be grateful, as we have had cause to be grateful in the past, that with all its weaknesses, with all its frustrations, with all its failures, the United Nations, the world organization, is in existence today, and stands between humanity and destruction. I think we can also be grateful that the United States, which is the world's most powerful state, has not hesitated to bring this matter before the United Nations so that its action and its conduct can be considered by the representatives of 109 nations and a decision can be reached in the world forum as to that action.
Mr. Speaker, it has been said that what is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander. When we hear statements like that it is perhaps just as well to remember that in 1956, when the Soviet union attacked Hungary with fire, sword and terror, the Soviet union did not bring its action to the attention of the United Nations. As many hon. members of this house know, it rejected the right of the United Nations even to look into that action. So, Mr. Speaker, while we can be grateful indeed for the United Nations intervention in this matter, I think we can also be grateful for the action taken by the United States in bringing its action to the United Nations. I think we can support, as the United Kingdom has supported and in every appropriate way, the position of the United States at the United Nations.
As I have already said, that does not mean, in the minds of many people, that all the details of that action are to be approved without qualification. Many people, friends of the United States and anxious to support the United States, may question some of the arguments used and indeed some of the action taken. But while that may be true, that is not so important as the necessity of rallying round our neighbour and our friend as members of the North Atlantic alliance around a friend which is a free and democratic nation; where there is an open society, where people can make up their minds and public opinion can express itself; which has a society that is not imperialistic in design and is not imperialistic in action.

Mr. Speaker, I think it must be an encouragement to all of us that the position I suggest should be taken, to which the Prime Minister has already referred, is a position taken by every member of the organization of American states, a good many of whom have been critical of many aspects of United States policy in Latin America and indeed in Cuba. It is a comforting fact and it makes, I think, for peace and security, that the western hemisphere is united in the broad issue before the United Nations in this present threat to peace and security.
There is one other aspect of the question which the Prime Minister has mentioned. The United Nations has intervened. The secretary general, in a way which reminds us of the attitude adopted by his great predecessor, has intervened with wisdom and restraint and has put forward to the security council on behalf of, I think, 44 Asian and African members-a great number of Asian and African members-a proposal which may prevent the situation from deteriorating while a solution for the broad problems can be found.
Very often-and the history of the past world war has shown this-it takes this kind of crisis in order to find solutions which go beyond the crisis itself. So perhaps out of this danger and out of this threat we can find solutions to problems which it would have been impossible to find in other atmospheres. The secretary general has perhaps shown us how this can be done. He has indicated that the United Nations could intervene at this time through a resolution which is a kind of stand-still resolution, under which the United States would abandon its blockade and the U.S.S.R. would abandon the shipment of military supplies to Cuba for a period of time. During that period of time perhaps a solution can be found, not only to the immediate problem but to related and perhaps even more important problems.
This seems to me to be a very constructive and encouraging development. But I suggest that it would have far more chance of success if it could be supplemented by some proposal which would ensure that any obligation undertaken by those concerned would be carried out. The particular proposal indicates that there would be an obligation on the United States to abandon the blockade, which obligation could not be broken without it being known at once. It is almost a self-enforcing obligation. But the obligation on the other side, not to send military supplies to Cuba, is one that could be evaded unless there were facilities for control and inspection.
There is something therefore that the Canadian delegation, if the opportunity arises

at the United Nations, could do. There could be a supplementary proposal to set up immediately a United Nations naval inspection force to make sure that any obligation of this kind, undertaken with a view to giving time and opportunity for finding a solution to the basic problem, was carried out. While that is being done a United Nations naval inspection force could be brought into action to reassure people who might question whether the word of a Soviet government should be accepted, even in respect of an obligation of this kind. This would give the kind of reassurance which United Nations inspection and control has given in the past and which I think could be given in the future.
This is one possibility that might improve the situation, and I have no doubt there are others. It is good to know that the Canadian government in this situation is working, as it is working, to bring about a strengthening of peace and security, to remove the awful threat of war. It is good to know that the Canadian government is right behind our friend and neighbour, the United States, in this issue.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed reassuring to us in this house, as I believe it is also to all Canadian people and as it will be to the friends of peace across the world, to hear the Prime Minister speak in the terms he has just used. I think one of the basic prerequisites of peace in our time is that we realize and understand the obligation we have to our friends and neighbours. It is only as we stand together with those who hold the same ideals and cherish the same way of freedom that we have in this country that we can have any hope of standing against the onslaught of communism in our time.
There can be no compromise between right and wrong; let us understand that. Coexistence with communism, in the end, means submission. But the objective of submission held by the ideological forces which oppose us at this time is not to be gained through the use of force, even as a bully in a school yard attempts to gain his way by force over his school mates. It is to be gained through a neutralizing of resistance, through passiveness. I believe there is no intolerance so vicious and so strong in reaching its objective as the intolerance of neutrality. I am pleased to hear the leader of the government, the Prime Minister, speak as he has spoken in this regard. The brain washing technique reaches its objective through the neutralizing of resistance so far as the mental attitudes of its victims are concerned.
Crisis in Cuba
Let us remember that we are a nation. We are a sovereign nation, a nation that has every right to be proud of its heritage. We are a nation that today has its responsibility, a responsibility which will increase with every passing day in all the tomorrows. This does not mean hostility or an attitude of contentiousness toward those who are on the other side of the fence.
I believe we as Canadians have a great potential to take a quiet, determined stand on what we know is right, and for which the world today looks in its quest for peace.
I am also sure we all agree that the efforts being put forward at present by the United Nations are most important. It is again reassuring to know that our delegation at the United Nations is doing everything within its power to further the action taken by the United Nations and the influence which the United Nations can have at this time.
In addition to the direct approach of the United Nations, which is now taking place, there is also a real opportunity for us to use our influence among those nations which may not be committed in the same way we are. Many of us individually probably have the opportunity to do this in what may seem to be little ways, but as a nation we have a great opportunity. Let us remember that the cost of friendship is friendliness, and friendliness is a force we must use at every opportunity.
It is also gratifying to note the unanimity that has been expressed through the organization of American states, and I suggest to the government that this is an ideal time for us to take our stand with our neighbours in this hemisphere and become a participating member in that organization. Certainly the first step could be taken in that regard by very determinedly making our own influence felt and moving in that direction now.
Let us just not say we are backing the United States and then sit down, pat ourselves on the back and think we have done something. We as Canadians have respect for our own sovereignty, and we support the United States as our friends and best neighbours. We do not do so as a vassal state or as a weak neighbour. We do it because we are Canadians, citizens of the sovereign state of Canada. Let us stand together in this house as Canadians. Let us stand together on our policy as Canadians, remembering that we do not have to bend ourselves to all the whims of those who are much more powerful than we are. Let us remember that we have an opportunity to give leadership at this time and, as the leader of the official opposition stated, perhaps it takes a crisis like this to bring out that leadership. Today the world is looking for leadership, leadership other than that

Crisis in Cuba
which is being given by the two great opposing forces in this world conflict. As Canadians we have an opportunity to give hope and leadership to many of the smaller nations that are not able to stand as we do today. Let us make sure we fulfill our obligation in that regard.
Let us also remember that in this chess game of international politics, where one nation is lined up against another on either side of the wall that divides us into two camps, we are not dealing just with nations that are represented by governments. We are dealing with governments that in themselves are representative of millions and millions of people, people like you and I, people who need to live and who want to live, people who look for peace as we do, and among them are the people on the other side of the fence. As we try to solve our problems and speak about these things, let us remember we are doing so on behalf of millions of people whose lives mean as much to them as do ours to us.
I was reminded of a statement the other day, which perhaps it is fitting to use here, and which says "It is better to be fed than red." In this context we have a chance to give leadership in our own hemisphere, a chance to reach out at this time to those nations that are not so fortunate as we are, and through our tremendous potential for good will and material wealth, provide those things which are necessary for people to live. Also it is to see what more we can do for our neighbours to draw them into that neighbourhood of nations which can do so much in the western hemisphere. Let us move on to assist many of the countries in Latin America which need assistance and which are looking for leadership.
In this crisis every red blooded Canadian understands that the issues are grave. Actually we are at war. We have not wanted to admit that down through the years, but the cold war we have been fighting during the last 12 years-indeed, since the end of world war I if we care to go back that far-is just as much a war and is just as grave as any war in which we have been involved. It is a war not necessarily fought with armed military might, but the forces used are just as decisive in the end.
Therefore in our struggle and our quest for peace we come back again to the issue which has been exemplified in the statement given us today by the Prime Minister. We must stand with our friends for what is right, and we must do everything possible to develop and further cultivate the peace which this world must have if it is to survive at all.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since my statement on Monday evening last, which I made on behalf of this party, in which I briefly outlined our general approach to the Cuban crisis and emphasized our hopes, the members of this party have had an opportunity to obtain the facts, to obtain information, and to assess that information and those facts. Let me emphasize that members of this group come to their decisions with the knowledge of their responsibility to the Canadian people and their responsibility to the many millions of people referred to by the leader of the party opposite.
We had hoped to present our views to the house before now, particularly yesterday which we thought would have been a most appropriate opportunity, being United Nations day, to give a detailed exposition of our views with respect to this most unfortunate crisis. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, we welcome this opportunity to make a statement on the Cuban crisis in line with our long time over-all policy on external affairs.
Members of the house know the policy of this group with respect to disarmament, with respect to nuclear weapons, with respect to nuclear testing, and they know the confidence and faith which this group has expressed in the United Nations as the body to which all these problems should be directed.
I wish to emphasize that we seek no partisan advantage from this unfortunate crisis, but present our views and our proposals in the firm conviction that they are in the best interests of the Canadian people and will make a contribution toward the promotion of world peace.
Some people still cling to the fetish that Canadians must never rock the boat of United States foreign policy. With that point of view the members of this party differ sharply, and we consider it our duty and responsibility to suggest another course when we believe that the present one is likely to land us on the rocks of international suicide.
In our opinion, Mr. Speaker, the present course being pursued by the United States may result in a propaganda victory for Mr. Khrushchev and mark him as a peacemaker in the eyes of many nations in the world. I might direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that even today's editorial in the Globe and Mail suggests this. If I may quote briefly from that editorial it says:
He can pose as the peacemaker turning the other cheek to United States aggression.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that we agree with the remarks of the leader of the official opposition with respect to the tragic situation that occurred in Hungary. But also

let me say that two wrongs do not make a right. Let me emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that our party has always been opposed to unilateral action by any power. Therefore on that account we regret Soviet action in installing missile bases in Cuba, and we are very critical and unhappy about the fact that the United States government has decided upon a course of action which could easily lead to the most serious consequences without first bringing the whole matter of these missile bases to the attention of the United Nations.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it would seem to me from answers given by the Prime Minister to questions asked in this house that the government of our friendly and powerful neighbour decided on its course of action without consulting its nearest neighbour, Canada, or its NATO allies, but merely informed them of the action decided upon. I emphasize-and no one can properly contradict me-that this is a flagrant violation of the terms of the north Atlantic treaty. The President of the United States has ignored the consultative machinery of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Its members were not asked for their opinion or advice; they were simply and baldly told what the United States intended to do, and to that course of action in the present world situation we take the strongest exception.
The Cuban situation has, of course, highlighted two or three present international problems. It has served to underline the correctness of our policy in opposing the spread of nuclear weapons, and therefore opposing nuclear weapons on our soil or in the hands of Canadians elsewhere. It is abundantly clear that the security of Cuba has been seriously harmed by the installation of nuclear bases, and that the threat to peace has been immensely increased. This is precisely the result which the New Democratic party has foreseen would inevitably follow the spread of nuclear weapons, and this is why we have consistently and strongly opposed any further dispersal of nuclear arms on the part of anyone. The installation of Soviet bases on Cuban soil has also focused attention on the fact that there are United States bases, and those of other nations, in many lands across the world, bases which are considered an ever present threat by others-and we can understand that-as the bases in Cuba are considered to be on this continent.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in all seriousness we urge that the crisis which has been created in recent days should be used by all nations, including the U.S.S.R. and the United States, to grapple with the whole problem of military bases, and particularly nuclear ones, and to
Crisis in Cuba
seek a policy of gradual dismantling of such bases everywhere as another step toward disarmament. The crisis in the Caribbean has served to take off the front pages of our newspapers the reports of fighting on the Indian-Chinese border, but we must recognize that that conflict is a part of the general unrest in the world today. It is another example of unilateral action by a nation, this time communist China, against a friendly neighbour. Unfortunately, however, Mr. Speaker, it is not possible to take the usual steps in the United Nations to condemn China's action in the Himalayas and demand a cessation of hostilities there, because the People's Republic of China has not been admitted to, and is not a member of, the United Nations. This is a matter which I think we have cause to regret at this time and will continue to regret under the developing circumstances of the world.
However, it is not enough merely to regret what has happened, from the point of view of the members of this party. We must find a way out; and my major purpose, Mr. Speaker, in rising on behalf of this group today is to make some positive proposals. There are some who say that the United Nations is helpless when conflicts occur between large powers. This party is not prepared to accept that, because there is no other road to peaceful settlement of international disputes except that provided by the machinery of the United Nations.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we propose that Canada should immediately seek support for a resolution to be presented at the security council and, if necessary, later to the assembly of the United Nations, under the terms of the special resolution respecting uniting for peace, that would look for the removal of the immediate threat to peace in the Caribbean so that time might be bought for necessary negotiations-and time is the essence of this very dangerous situation.
We claim, Mr. Speaker, that such a resolution should propose that the U.S.S.R. and the U.S.A. act immediately and simultaneously to turn Soviet ships away from the direction of Cuba and to remove the United States blockade from the Caribbean. If that is accepted it might be necessary to have some ships from other countries police the shipping lanes to make certain that the two big powers carried out their undertakings.
Mr. Speaker, the members of this group, and I may say many members in this house, were very pleased to see in the Gazette this morning the request by U Thant asking the U.S. and the U.S.S.R. hold up on Cuba, making a proposal somewhat similar to the one we are making today to which we gave consideration some days ago. Such a United

Crisis in Cuba
Nations resolution should also include a section which recognizes in the strongest terms the integrity of Cuba and seeks to remove any fears which Cubans have, and which we can understand, as a result of past actions.
In our party's view, some such concrete and positive step must be taken by the United Nations. The world organization has succeeded in limiting and in stopping local conflicts. It has done excellent work in that respect throughout the years when smaller nations were involved. It is now facing the supreme test as to whether it can be effective also when the two great powers are concerned. No one can believe, Mr. Speaker, that either the United States or the Soviet union would wilfully risk the destruction which would occur from a thermonuclear war. In this, in our opinion, lies the hope that energetic, prompt and constructive action by the smaller powers, such as Canada, through our government, and through the United Nations may not only save the world from the horrors which threaten it, but may also begin to lay the basis for a stronger world organization and for a lasting peace.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that if the Cuban crisis has done nothing else it has underlined in such a terrifying way the frightful peril in which mankind has stood ever since the invention of nuclear weapons, and that at long last the whole world, including the two great nuclear powers, must be convinced that war is an impossibility unless the human race is prepared to commit suicide. This grim and frightening occasion must be seized on now, while the terror is fresh in people's minds, as an opportunity to press forward with the dismantling of all missile bases throughout the world, which will mark the beginning of a permanent retreat from the awful abyss which opened up this week when the United States gambled with the lives of all of us in its struggle with the U.S.S.R.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, of which I have given him notice. I want to talk, basically, about the resolutions which we are shortly going to consider. Perhaps I will be excused if I make special reference to those dealing with the oil and gas industry, because I think, of the 15 resolutions, seven concern themselves with problems related to the development of our petroleum resources. Before doing this, however, I should like to draw the attention of the committee to the nature of these resolutions. They are basically designed to provide incentive to our development industries, to create new jobs, new production, new opportunities for Canadians. It seems to me that this is particularly significant and, I suggest, important, because in a day and age when a great many of us-in my view, too many of us-are looking to the state for a handout or for a particular support program, without return to the state, or for the establishment of some new social legislation, Canadians are bound to ask us how or when do we intend to repay the debt that is involved in each of these measures.
I know it is said, as a rule of thumb, I think, that for every 1 per cent increase in gross national production there is a return of revenue to the extent of $100 million. The figure is not important. The fact is that if we build into our legislative system a series of grants or a series of social measures to the extent that they call upon the treasury to produce vast amounts of money, unless there is some check in the future it is my belief that we will end up as a nation whose people do little more than collect taxes from one another as an occupation.
Therefore I am happy to see this series of resolutions is designed to do two things. First of all, it is designed to provide encouragement for the development of one of our major industries; in fact, Canada's major mineral industry; second, to encourage Canadians to participate in its development. This house knows, of course, that this is not the first occasion we have turned our attention to the problems of the oil and gas industry. The history in five years is almost unbelievable.

First of all we established the Borden commission to make a review of the problems so that we could direct policy in recent years. Following the commission there was the establishment of the national energy board. This was the first time the industry could come before the government in a public forum to discuss its problems.
We then established the territories regulations, known as the Canadian oil and gas regulations, encouraging Canadians as never before to participate in their national resources. Following this was the highly successful national oil policy, a policy which has increased production for this year alone by more than 16 per cent. The processing of some 11 gas applications followed, and even the Department of Trade and Commerce, which one would not normally think would be in the field of research publications, has developed and assisted the industry, in providing a survey of its requirements in terms under which Canadians could determine the extent of oil field equipment that could be made in Canada.
I repeat this history because we are inclined to forget the extent to which this government has gone to assist one industry, and by so doing, recognizes the importance of this industry to the economy of Canada.
I have said, Mr. Chairman, that we have been successful over these four years. Perhaps I might put on the record certain references or statistics, as much as I dislike them, which justify this enthusiasm. As an example, in the field of gas export; in fact, in almost every field from gas export to petroleum production the percentages and volumes have surpassed even the enthusiasm of many of the people who developed the policy. Starting with gas, we have from the 293 billion cubic feet produced in 1957 increased this year to something over 735 billion cubic feet. Expressed another way, though-and this is what I suggest is relevant-crude oil and natural gas minerals in 1961 showed a 20 per cent increase; natural gas alone, something like 23 per cent. It will be considerably higher this year, of course.
The advent of new pipe line construction brought revenue up about 20 per cent; dollar value of oil exports, 62 per cent and gas exports, about 92 per cent. I think these figures clearly illustrate the nature of the policy of trying to encourage the development of this industry. The result, of course, has been exhibited in those figures. They show the success of the policy, one which certainly has merited this success.
Mr. Chairman, I want to talk about the resolutions themselves and to say a word to the minister, because I think he will agree with me that we must not be satisfied that we have in any way settled the long term 27507-3-59
Income Tax Act
problem which will continue to confront the petroleum industry. First of all, the resolutions are designed in the first part to broaden the activity of Canadians by permitting those whose primary business is not concerned with the petroleum industry to write off certain costs against income; second, to permit people to write off acquisition costs and production costs. In other words, these are incentives to encourage people to come into the industry in a substantial way.
I know a great many people will think these are indeed generous terms, but it must be remembered that when you calculate generosity it has to be measured in terms of the risk involved. Anyone who has been associated with petroleum development knows that a single well may cost $1 million or more to drill, and that if unsuccessful, the return is purely the bits and pieces of equipment you can pick up. One can then understand the necessity for providing incentives. Yet we have found this industry, in the last few years, suffering hardships even in face of the prosperity I have mentioned. We have even seen a great many small, independent companies being absorbed by major companies. In fact, in the last 18 months ten of these smaller companies, Canadian operations well known in the foothills of Alberta, have been absorbed by foreign corporations.
Mr. Chairman, I want to examine briefly why this has happened and suggest to the minister the sort of action that should be taken to preserve the opportunities still further for Canadians. Second, I wish to conclude on a note as to future policy, an extension of the present oil policy. I do not think we need be alarmed by the fact that we have lost some ten independent companies, so long as we recognize how this occurred. I do not think we should ask any government or any company to maintain a purely Canadian identity of any corporation based on pure sentimentality. It just does not make sense. It is a very nice thing for the Canadian ego to say we have "x" number of Canadian companies competing in the Canadian oil industry, but unless we are prepared to support them by some measures such as these resolutions, such a statement is meaningless.
We have lost some ten Canadian companies by the very nature of the fact that oil in the ground today has a greater value than it has had at any other time. While we are producing more oil, and the figures have indicated this as a result of the national oil policy, it is equally true that the rate of discovery of oilfields is alarmingly lower, for in the last two years no major oilfields have been found.

These resolutions introduced by the minister are designed to encourage and speed up exploration so that we can return to a more proper ratio between reserves and production.
When we look at the Canadian companies which have gone, and which we hope will be replaced by others, we must ask ourselves if there is any other reason why they have disappeared. The second reason is that, with the success of new cash from the sale of gas and increased oil production, it is quite apparent that they become more attractive investments to major companies. This too has been a major factor in major companies buying out small independents. In addition it has been just good business. When a shareholder of a Canadian company can be offered double or triple the value for his shares or equity, then naturally he is prepared to sell them.
What then can we do to correct this trend? First of all, I think we should not be concerned about those companies which have been absorbed. A great many of them have been integrated into foreign companies, and, for the first time, Canadians are being offered an opportunity to participate in their world wide, international operations, through share purchases on Canadian exchanges. This too, I suggest, has been at the persuasion and with the enthusiastic support of the present government. Second, many of these companies have completely integrated their Canadian counterparts into their own operations so that there has been no loss to Canadian employment in this respect.
I believe that if we are to encourage further opportunities for Canadian companies to compete, we must judge the present resolutions to see that we have actually broadened the basis upon which Canadians can participate in the development of Canadian oil, and upon which new Canadian companies will be formed. I believe this is the key resolution. The only suggestion I make to the minister is that after the operation of the resolution for a year he might consider whether or not it would be beneficial to extend that right of write-off against all the operation of their principle business and not merely provide for a write-off for those oil companies in which they are participating. I would suggest that if this were done it would encourage more Canadians, with their investment capital, to go further into the development of the petroleum industry.
All of us recognize that in losing some of our independent companies we have also lost identity with a great many of those pioneers who, for so long, were responsible for the development of the gas and oil industries in Canada. It is true that while they may not

have developed the majority of the fields that have been in existence for some time, they have nevertheless been responsible for more than their share in the discovery of oil fields, because an independent company cannot sit on oil reserves. It must have continuing reserves and therefore must go out and wildcat and make new discoveries.
It is an advantage to this government, and to the Canadian people as a whole, to encourage Canadian independence under any circumstances. It not only has the advantage of employing more Canadian people but it provides Canadian investment capital to underwrite industry, and as has been their job in past years, to find what is so urgently required today, and that is the discovery of a major oil field.
I believe the resolutions are designed with this object in mind, to provide incentive and encouragement, because they are providing risk capital with the opportunity of writing off that risk against income. I say to the minister that this is one of the first positive steps made in many years designed to assist where assistance is required most, in the making available of new capital.
Now, may I say a word or two about the national oil policy? I read with interest the comments of one of the distinguished hon. members opposite who spoke on this subject. He discussed the importance and the necessity of taking some action either in finding new markets for Canadian oil in Canada, or in increasing our exports abroad. I cannot disagree with his sentiment but I wish to say one or two things about it.
The hon. member for Davenport had this to say:
Steps should be taken to bring our imports and exports of oil and petroleum products into balance.
This is a good, safe statement and no one can argue with it. He also said:
I know that some progress has been made in this direction, but a great deal more should be done, and it should be done quickly.
I would also agree with him that a great deal more can be done, but it is interesting to note one of the comparisons he made. He said:
In 1961, last year, our imports of crude oil and petroleum products exceeded our exports by some $137 million and if natural gas Is included in the calculations, and I do not believe it should, our adverse balance still exceeded $100 million.
These figures, of course, are correct, but it is interesting to note that this is still less than a third of the figure of two years ago, so that we have made considerable progress and are continuing to make more.

Let us look and examine his statement still further. He suggests:
Either we should Increase our exports very considerably or we should take another serious, hard look at the case for an all-Canadian oil pipe line from Alberta to Ontario and Quebec.
May I reiterate the steps which we have taken by way of legislation, and remind the committee that this was the same problem which confronted the Borden commission, and which was discussed at some length on the introduction of the National Energy Board Act?
At that time it was decided that the best way to increase Canadian production, with the least interference by government, was to try to encourage the oil industry to work out its own problems. The companies were called together with a view to discussing which course we should take, and how certain minimum production figures could be reached.
I complimented the government earlier in that their target for 1961 was easily accomplished. They will exceed their 1962 target by a considerable degree and there is no question but that the oil target for next year, 1963, will also be surpassed. However, it is also fair to say that this target in the latter two years will be reached with a considerable part of it, approximately a third of it, entering the United States market both in the midwest and in district 5 of the Pacific northwest.
Therefore we can agree the policy has been successful, but the hon. member for Davenport suggests, as one alternative, that we further increase our exports into the United States. I know he is aware of the concern expressed by the secretary of the interior of the United States regarding any substantial increases in the import of oil into that country. I know he has read, as I have, the repeated statements by major independent organizations, principally the independent petroleum association of the United States, encouraging congress and the president of the United States to put Canada in terms of quota, as are other countries which export oil into the United States. Therefore it seems to me that if we adopt this suggestion and rapidly increase our exports to the United States, we may find the United States taking that action which it took some two years ago against many other countries, and cutting off our oil exports entirely.
What of his other suggestion of having a pipe line to Montreal? This has a certain odd advantage which he points out, in terms of Canada's exchange with the United States; and in terms of the construction of a line it would employ many Canadians and would also add to Canadian security by making it free from dependency on crude oil from the Middle East or Venezuela. Yes, there is much 27507-3-59J

to be said for a Montreal pipe line. In fact, the first speech I made in this house in 1957 advocated that such a line would and should be built as a matter of course. I believe I said on that occasion that it was only a question of time. The government, however, decided not to build the Montreal pipe line but made provision in a section of the energy board act to construct the line if the national oil policy was not a success. The national oil policy can be a success-but it must be dependant entirely upon the development of new Canadian markets, not on exports-only if the industry continues as it has in the past two years, and I emphasize that it has cooperated in developing new markets in the Montreal area and in the extension of the present Ontario area. If this is accomplished, it is my belief that it is not for some time that we will need either to increase exports to the United States or to construct the Montreal pipe line.
But having said that, and having believed that the extension of the present national oil policy should be made in the near future so that oil companies, the industry, and all those associated can make their plans and projections for the years ahead, I still have one concern about the present oil policy. I said that it was dependant upon Canadian oil companies, particularly the integrated refiners, taking the greater part of Canadian oil production, refining it and distributing it in the large Montreal markets. It was not dependant on the United States accepting increased volume of Canadian crude. But it is quite obvious that this year and in subsequent years the export market into the midwest and the Pacific northwest is to a very large degree going to play an important role in our oil policy. My one concern is that if any of the pressures which have currently been brought to bear in Washington on the President of the United States are successful, and further, if there is any attempt to create embargoes against Canadian products, then it becomes automatic that we have to invoke the assistance of the national oil policy and construct this Montreal pipe line.
Mr. Chairman, in the history of our relationship with the United States in the exchange of goods, we have seen a series of situations which shows that when the United States reaches a stage of oversupply of any particular product or resource from Canada, pressures within that country-and this is understandable-are brought to bear on the president suggesting to him that they should block a particular Canadian product. We have seen it happen with uranium, with lead and zinc, and now with lumber. It is conceivable that such pressures could build up against oil

going into the two areas of the United States, and if that is the case I would have real concern about the success of the national oil policy. Because it would mean we would have to find a new home for over 200,000 barrels a day of Canadian oil. So I say to you, Mr. Chairman, and to hon. gentlemen in this committee, that I believe we should attempt to reach some understanding with the chief executive of the United States as to what is the attitude of their government with respect to all Canadian resources.
I said previously that I had hoped we could get either an understanding in a contractual agreement-a letter of intent-or something in the form of a treaty. Perhaps I am being a little na'ive and such an agreement might prove to be too inflexible; but I see the need for at least some understanding between our two heads of state or a discussion of the whole question of the exchange of resource products, so that we do not find ourselves in a year or six months time in the position where they will say to us: "I am sorry, but the lobby of the independent petroleum oil operators of the United States has become extreme and we find it necessary to restrict or to cut out entirely the quota of oil entering the United States". It seems unlikely that such a course would be adopted, especially in view of President Kennedy's recent trade bill; but nevertheless it is significant to note that two committees have been studying just this subject in the United States. One of these committees completed its study recently and reported, indicating that the United States, of course, requires the continued supply of natural gas from Canada; but they are not this anxious about accepting our oil.
I can understand the attitude of the American oil industry. Quite obviously, with oil going into areas which their producers could normally supply, this in turn slows up their desire to find new fields and incentive is reduced. But let us look also at the Canadian industry. We are taking into eastern Canada about one third of our total capacity. We have increased production in several areas, and while there is a shortage of oil today and a shortage of reserves, there is surely no desire by the Canadian oil industry to look for new reserves unless they realize that they are going to be able to market this oil. So I repeat that we cannot leave the Canadian oil industry in a state of indecision, not knowing from day to day whether or not they are going to have the door closed on a large part of their present market.
I believe that it is essential that the Prime Minister and President Kennedy discuss this as but one related matter in the exchange of all our resource products. I emphasize "all"

of them, because I think it is important to note that while we are in a position to bargain and to say to our friends that we are anxious to provide them with many of these products, we should remind ourselves of the fact that if the U.S. runs into another deficient position of oversupply their desire to bargain becomes somewhat more apparent. I believe we can serve the purpose both of United States oil marketers and the Canadian industry, as well as the Canadian government, by having a clear and frank understanding as to the direction in which we are going.
Now, sir, I want to close on just about the note I began. We have come a long way in the development of our resources. We have provided encouragement and incentive in these resolutions. It is absolutely essential that these resolutions pass this committee at an early date in order to make certain that Canadians can go into this area of resource development with a clear understanding of the risk which is involved with their capital investment, and realizing that they will have every encouragement from this government to carry out their undertakings. I believe it is equally important that the government should keep a very close watch to determine whether or not they have in these resolutions gone far enough to achieve this objective. Third, I would hope the government would at an early date clearly indicate in which direction a national oil policy will go, and what the industry may expect in new targets after 1963. These targets should be projected soon so that the industry may plan to meet them. May I, as one who for so long has been interested in this particular subject, pay my respects to the members of the cabinet concerned, and particularly to those members of the civil service, especially Mr. McKinnon, the chairman of the national energy board, who has for so long and so diligently negotiated, and successfully negotiated, Canada's present inter-relationship with the United States on all of these problems. In closing, I would say only that I have talked about the need for incentives to encourage industry. This is the keynote, I suggest, of the present session-to increase production, to increase opportunities for Canadians to participate, and thus to create a better Canada, with more employment, and more encouragement to take part in their own natural resources.

Mr. Chairman, as this is the first time I have spoken in the house, perhaps I could take this opportunity to congratulate Mr. Speaker and Mr. Deputy Speaker upon their appointments and to thank them and the other officials of the house for the kindness and consideration they have shown to me and to other new members.

I have the honour to live in and represent the riding of St. Paul's, which is in the centre of Toronto, and which was previously represented in the house by the former Speaker, the Hon. Roland Michener. I was particularly pleased to hear at the beginning of this session the tributes which were paid to Mr. Michener by members of all parties in this house. I refer particularly to the statement made by the Prime Minister when he implied that had Mr. Michener been re-elected an opportunity would have been given to this House of Commons to consider the question of a permanent Speaker. As many hon. members will know, Mr. Michener announced last week that he would not be running for reelection in St. Paul's as he felt it would be inappropriate for one who had been a nonpartisan Speaker to run again as a private member. I hope the opportunity will be found to secure for his country the services of this gifted man in some other capacity.
Perhaps I might say just this with regard to the question of a permanent Speaker, which was debated quite vigorously in St. Paul's immediately prior to the election. Quite clearly I would think it would be desirable to have a more permanent Speaker, provided due provision is made for alternation between a Speaker who is primarily French speaking and one who is primarily English speaking. If this House of Commons has the will to do it, it can very easily be done by a very simple amendment to the provision in the British North America Act which now requires that the Speaker be a sitting member of the house. I speak subject to correction but, as I understand it, such an amendment could be made by this parliament without the concurrence of the provinces. I would suggest to hon. members that it is too much to expect that a Speaker, with the onerous duties that he has, and they are quite obvious to all of us, should be called upon also to represent a riding as a partisan.
In speaking at this time I have this advantage, Mr. Chairman, it is neither necessary nor desirable for me to waste the time of the house in criticizing the actions of the government. Let me therefore merely summarize by saying that we on this side of the chamber have moved several motions of no confidence. We did so because we sincerely believe that the ministry has failed the country in certain vital matters. Very briefly and without being provocative may I say that it has failed the country first in that it has failed to recognize that emergency problems of a very serious nature are facing the country. In the second place it has failed the country in that it has not accepted the responsibility as a federal government of

dealing with those problems. In the third place it has failed the country because it has refused to accept the necessity of developing plans which would adequately cope with those problems. That is all I will say on that score.
Having said that I would go on to say that we must recognize the fact that the government has done many things which are of value to Canada. As one who was born in Saskatchewan and grew up there I was happy to learn that the government had decided to proceed and was proceeding vigorously with the South Saskatchewan dam. Whatever the economics of that project may be, I am convinced that it will be of tremendous value to the people of Saskatchewan where water in ample supply is both a necessity and a luxury too frequently lacking.
Then again we are happy that western grain sales have been quite high in recent years. I commend the Minister of Agriculture for his enthusiasm and initiative in that respect, although we do not see how he can possibly expect complete approval of the house for his policies until such time as he has divulged to the house the terms upon which the sales of western grain have been made to communist countries and the extent to which the people of Canada are financing the purchase of such grain. Surely this is something the house is entitled to know.
Again, the concept of northern development, many of us believe, is an extremely important and valuable one. However, we feel that it is not being carried out adequately. The vision-and I say this seriously-must be translated into actuality. After all, Canada's north is our last frontier. It is a great Canadian heritage. I am sure all of us will agree that those thousands of square miles of Canada's northland cannot be held for this country merely by declarations in this House of Commons or by extending lines on a map from our southern boundary. All history shows that the only way in which that country can be held for future generations of Canadians is by populating it or putting people there. It is my understanding that the government has indicated that $100 million may be appropriated for the centennial celebration. I would seriously suggest that this money, instead of being spent on monuments or pomp and ceremony, be spent to a great extent in establishing and maintaining a circle of outposts in the north and in keeping Canadians there in order to ensure that this part of the country will always remain Canadian.
No doubt there are other valuable policies which the government has carried out. At this point 1 should just like to emphasize two

things. The first is that the four points I picked out and mentioned all involve governmental planning. The second point I should like to make is that while everyone in the house recognizes the importance of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta, I should like to remind the minister that there are other provinces in Canada, notably the great province of British Columbia to the west and the great provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland to the east. These provinces also should be given the benefits of governmental economic planning.
In reviewing the record of Hansard to date many of us are a bit concerned by the fact that many of the statements made by the ministers exhibit a certain feeling of complacency and lack of a sense of urgency. For example, I find in Hansard quotations taken from every and any source, whether expert or not, in order to prove that everything is fine and that we have no very serious or basic problems. We find, for example, statements such as these: the forecast is fine for Canada; the economy is rolling along; Canada has a clean and glowing bill of economic health; the economy is on the up and up.
As I read that I could not help thinking of that old slogan which Dr. Coue made so famous years ago: Every day in every way we are getting better and better. So I looked at the Encyclopaedia Britannica to find out what it had to say about Dr. Coue and I should like to read this extract into the record:
Emile Coue (1857-1926), French psychotherapist whose formula "every day, and in every way, X am becoming better and better" became proverbial. Based on the power of imagination rather than that of the will, his na'ive and empiric system utilized formulas, repeated again and again in a confident voice, especially at a time when the mind was most receptive, to sink into the subconscious and to eliminate ideas tending to cause distress and disease.
But then I realized that these statements were made in the debate on the speech from the throne and I did not really become concerned until the Minister of Finance delivered his budget speech last Monday evening. As I listened to him then, I really began to wonder whether I was completely sane or whether something had gone completely wrong and I was in some sort of wonderland. For the benefit of the new members and also for the benefit of those who will come after us I should like to put on the record something I found in browsing through the library that gave me a great deal of comfort. I think I have come upon the explanation and it is that the ministers of the government have been engaging in what is called "doublethink".

All hon. members will remember that "doublethink", as defined by that great philosopher, Emmanuel Goldstein, in his work on "The Theory and Practice of Oligarchical Collectivism", was quoted by George Orwell in his work, "Nineteen Eighty four" on pages 214 and 215. I should like to quote a lot of it because it is most helpful but I must refrain and only quote a little. I recommend the work to all hon. members. It reads:
"Doublethink" means the power of holding two contradictory beliefs in one's mind simultaneously, and accepting both of them. The party intellectual knows in which direction his memories must be altered; he therefore knows that he is playing tricks with reality; but by the exercise of "doublethink" he also satisfies himself that reality is not violated. The process has to be conscious, or it would not be carried out with sufficient precision, but it also has to be unconscious, or it would bring with it a feeling of falsity and hence of guilt. ...to forget any fact that has become inconvenient, and then, when it becomes necessary again, to draw it back from oblivion for just so long as it is needed, to deny the existence of objective reality and all the while take account of the reality which one denies-all this is indispensably necessary. Even in using the word "doublethink" it is necessary to exercise "doublethink". For by using the word one admits that one is tampering with reality; by a fresh act of "doublethink" one erases this knowledge; and so on indefinitely, with the lie always one leap ahead of the truth.
I have read this into the record merely to assist all those who, like myself, are new members and also those who may follow us in the years to come. It was a great consolation to me. As I say, I became deeply concerned only when I listened to the speech of the Minister of Finance, particularly when he came to this point and said, as found on page 808 of Hansard:
-we Canadians are living in the most prosperous year in Canada's history.

Then we can only take it that this was not inadvertent and that the minister was really aware that this statement was in fact in the prepared text. That is very serious because it is of tremendous importance that Canada's Minister of Finance should recognize that this country has basic problems and not just a balance of payments problem, because if he does not recognize that he will be unable to find appropriate solutions.
What are these basic problems? In human terms let me tell all hon. members that within five minutes walk of the corner of Bay and King streets which is the heart of the financial district in Toronto, you will find forced unemployment on a massive scale, disease, poverty, hunger and despair. If anyone here thinks that is not true I will be happy to take him to my riding of St. Paul's and show him some of the areas in the southern portion of it.
Those are real human problems. If human problems have no effect upon the ministers, let me translate these human problems into other terms which may have some effect upon them. What are some of these problems? First, at this moment hundreds of thousands of Canadians, our fellow citizens, are suffering from forced unemployment. Second, business failures and bankruptcies are at an all-time high. Third, more people are leaving Canada this year than are entering, and the ones who are leaving are our most highly skilled and valuable citizens. Fourth, the cost of living continues to rise. Fifth, the value of our dollar has gone down. Sixth, production per capita in Canada has actually declined in recent years. Seventh, in five years our federal government has spent about $4 billion more than it has taken in, according to my arithmetic, made up of $3 billion in deficits and approximately $1 billion in diminution of the unemployment insurance fund. Those are the problems translated from the human to less human terms. Perhaps they will make the ministers think, and not "doublethink".
What should we do about this problem? The government has told us that they hope to provide, over the next four years, about

Perhaps I was asleep at the time and did not hear that. I see that I have only five minutes left, so I would like to get these ideas across, though they may not be new to hon. members on the other side, and I should like to get them on the record.
The idea is simply this, that the government should look at one industry after the other in Canada and develop a plan specifically tailored to each industry so that, over a period of time, approximately 50 per cent of Canada's present imports of manufactured goods will be replaced by a like amount of products manufactured in Canada. We on this side assert that this cannot be done and should not be done by surcharges or increased tariffs. We assert that this should be done by encouraging, and indeed requiring, every industry to adopt a plan similar to a plan adopted by Northern Electric to which reference was made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce earlier in the session.
My time is limited, but I should like to tell hon. members who have not seen this plan that a copy can be obtained from the minister's office. I may say the Minister of Trade and Commerce was sporting enough to say that this plan was conceived about six years ago which was, of course, when the Liberals were in power. However, this is irrelevant because the same thing can be done by the present ministry if they will follow this particular program.
Let me tell you what happened. Over a period of years Northern Electric found that they had built up what they called their import inventory. They developed the habit of importing items from other countries which were highly specialized. In 1956, the total number of items had grown to 8,000 or

Income Tax Act
9,000. They set up a committee first to consider these items to ascertain if they could not be produced in Canada. Then, they set up a committee of the higher brass to review the findings of the first committee. Then, a really top ranking man reviewed the findings of the second committee. Let me read to you what the results of that plan were by 1962:
The end result of our program was that we transferred to Canadian manufacture over this six year period, components which were costing us $11 million per year to import. This activity has resulted in the employment of about 1,600 Canadians.
This is one company we are talking about, and I assume they mean annual employment.
We made this $11 million worth at a substantial saving and tooling costs were recovered in about twelve months of production. A number of the parts were made in our own factory, but several thousand were subcontracted to other Canadian manufacturers.
I hope I am not being presumptuous when I suggest that the minister could go through this volume which is put out by the bureau of statistics and which shows what we are importing by industries, classify those industries and develop for each industry a plan along the lines of the Northern Electric plan. You have done it already in your national oil policy. This is exactly the type of thing I have in mind. If we had not had a national oil policy, Canadian oil production would not be as high as it is now. All I am suggesting is that you do the same thing for all these other industries, but do it on a collective basis and try to avoid the creation of governmental boards. The national oil policy, for a number of reasons, required the creation of boards, but many of these other industries would not. We should put the prime responsibility upon private business itself to develop a plan, and have a definite objective, namely an over-all replacement of 50 per cent.
Let me put it this way: The objective should be the replacement by Canadian products to the extent of 50 per cent of the value of the items we are now importing. I see I am running out of time, but I should like to say this, that statistics published by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association prove that each Canadian imports ten times as much in the way of manufactured goods as each citizen of the United States and six times as much as each Englishman. Now, this is almost incredible but it is true. If we reduce that amount by half, we would provide full employment for all Canadians.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ADDITIONAL AGREEMENTS
