I take if from that, Mr. Speaker, that I am not estopped from raising the point of order at this particular time. Then later that same day, October 1, at page 33 of Hansard Your Honour is reported as having said:
I have indicated with respect to all the bills now before us for consideration, they will be studied

Trans-Canada Highway Act
and prior to their introduction for second reading a ruling will be given by the Chair in respect of the said bills.
Again, to this the house agreed. Mr. Speaker, the point I am making is that the bill in question introduced by the hon. member for Skeena, Bill No. C-ll, to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act (Canada highways) is what is known by long and honourable usage as a money bill. So that my argument will be complete I would refer to the explanatory note of the bill, which says that the purpose of the bill is:
-to allow for the government of Canada financially to participate in the construction or improvement of any highway within a province, including a so-called second trans-Canada highway.
Mr. Speaker, I think by long usage it has been agreed that it is not possible for a private member, except in very rare cases where government itself may indicate its approval, to introduce such a bill as the hon. member for Skeena has brought before the house this afternoon. In support of this general proposition I refer you, Mr. Speaker to the fourth edition of Beauchesne's "Parliamentary Rules and Forms", page 204, citation 243:
All bills providing for the payment of salaries, or for any expenditure whatever out of the public funds of the dominion must be first considered as resolutions in committee of the whole. And all such resolutions necessary to the introduction of a bill must first obtain the recommendation of the governor general.
I think the records of the house will clearly show that up to this date, at least, we have had no recommendation from His Excellency read to the house, nor has a resolution which would precede the bill introduced by the hon. member been considered and passed by the committee of the whole.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I refer to a further citation in Beauchesne, page 214, citation 249. Here Dr. Beauchesne is quoting from a ruling of a previous clerk of the house, Mr. Bourinot:
No cases can be found of any private member in the Canadian commons receiving the authority of the crown, through a minister, to propose a motion involving the expenditure of public money. No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer. On one occasion, in the English commons, the consent of the crown was given to certain formal resolutions proposed by a private member with reference to charges in courts of law to be defrayed out of the consolidated fund-
That certainly has not happened in this case.
It was thought, however, that any resolution placing a charge on the consolidated fund should be moved by a minister of the crown, and the more regular procedure was thereupon carried out.
Therefore, even with the agreement of the House of Commons in Westminster, it was

decided to follow the safer course, the one which in effect has become constitutional usage.
It was distinctly affirmed, however, that the member who proposed the motion involving the charge was within his right when he had the sanction of the crown, but it was generally admitted at the same time that it was better, as a matter of policy, that the proposition should emanate from a responsible adviser of the sovereign.
The responsibility of recommending applications for pecuniary redress or relief-
This is from the same citation and deals with another matter, but none the less I feel it comes within the spirit of what one does when one is dealing with money.
-to the consideration of parliament should rest solely upon the executive government, who are strictly accountable for every item of public expenditure, whose especial duty it is, in the interest of the taxpayer, to oppose all unnecessary outlay, and who possess peculiar facilities for investigating into the merits of all pecuniary claims.
It is my submission, Mr. Speaker, that the case I bring before you now falls four square within that general principle. Then, on the next page of Beauchesne's there is citation 250 (1) which reads:
It seems that under section 11 of the British North America Act the Governor General cannot officially take advice in regard to public affairs from other persons than his sworn privy councillors. The section says:
"There shall be a council to aid and advise in the government of Canada, to be styled the Queen's privy council of Canada; and the persons who are to be members of that council shall be from time to time chosen and summoned by the Governor General and sworn in as privy councillors, and members thereof may be from time to time removed by the Governor General."
Dr. Beauchesne's comment on that is this:
The wording of this section makes it compulsory for the Governor General to consult his ministers, or at any rate privy councillors, before recommending to the house an expenditure sought by a private member.
That is exactly what has not happened here although an expenditure is sought by a private member. Then further on Dr. Beauchesne turned back to the English authorities, and in particular May:
If any motion, or bill, or proceeding is offered to be moved, whether in the house or in a committee, which requires, but fails to receive, the recommendation of the crown, it is the duty of the Chair to announce that no question can be proposed upon the motion, or to direct the withdrawal of the bill.
Again, sir, at page 216, citation 250(3) reads:
The object of the resolution recommended by the crown is to give the house a first opportunity to discuss the advisability of making a certain expenditure.
I suggest that the hon. member has bypassed this giving of the house such a first opportunity.

I was looking through Beauchesne to find some precedents on this matter. Unfortunately I could not find them in the few moments at my disposal since the point of order was raised, but my memory tells me this matter has been dealt with on other occasions and that there are precedents which rule in favour of a bill of this nature because it does not involve the expenditure of any money not authorized by parliament.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ADDITIONAL AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
If I may deal with the point raised by the hon. member as to whether it is a question of moneys being used in one direction or another that have been voted by parliament, under section 3 of the Trans-Canada Highway Act there is a provision:
With the approval of the governor in council the minister may enter into an agreement with any province providing for the payment by Canada to the province of contributions in respect of the cost to the province of the construction of a highway within the province as part of a trans-Canada highway.
I submit that only one thing can happen under that section, and that is that the minister charged with this responsibility enters into an agreement with a province, an agreement under which certain rights are defined and under which the province has to carry out certain contracts to allow it to receive a contribution from the federal treasury, and this contribution is put before us in the committee for our approval.
The hon. member has added "and other highways" to the section I have just read. That means to me, for example, that should my own province be building a highway in a part other than the part designated for a trans-Canada highway, there could be a charge upon the public purse here for the costs of that highway. Therefore I submit that the hon. member is not correct when he says that only a ceiling amount of money is involved which may go in one direction or another. I suggest, with deference, this is a matter of adding an extra expenditure on top of an already existing set-up.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PERMIT ADDITIONAL AGREEMENTS
speechtext:
A point of order has been raised as to whether this bill is within the power of the hon. member who introduced it as a private member, and whether it is contrary to the well accepted principle that a money bill can only be introduced by a minister of the crown after a proper resolution.
Now, having studied the matter, the fact is that the hon. member, by importing into this bill provisions in reliance on the Canada Highways Act, which was a 1919 statute, is trying to introduce an entirely new principle into the Trans-Canada Highway Act. He is trying to bring that measure within the scope of a bill which might be introduced by a private member by relying on the Canada Highways Act, which is chapter 54 of the statutes for 1919.
I do not think he can be successful in his endeavour for the following reasons. Briefly, section 3 of the old act of 1919 provided for an amount of $20 million during a period of five years from the first of April, 1919, so that the original act would have been valid only until 1924. However, in 1923-and I refer to chapter 4 of the statutes for that

Trans-Canada Highway Act year-there was an extension of the measure for another two years; and finally chapter 4 of the statutes of 1925 gave an extension for two more years. So on calculation, this bill was spent after those years, and the powers given to the government had lapsed unless there was to be a further extension, which did not take place.
It is well known that a minister of the government can introduce a measure to extend further the powers granted by the Canada Highways Act, 1919, and the amending acts of 1923 and 1925. I do not think it is sufficient to say, as does the hon. member, that the proposed amendment retains the present overall financial ceiling set by parliament, and the discretionary approval within that ceiling by the governor in council. All those bills of the government in 1919, 1923 and 1925 were introduced by resolutions. For instance, the act of 1923 was preceded by a resolution in committee of the whole which read as follows:
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide that the time within which the various provinces of Canada may earn and be paid the sums allotted to the said provinces under the provisions of "The Canada Highways Act", chapter 54 of the statutes of 1919, be extended for a further period of two years.
The resolution of 1925 was in similar form. Now, any attempt to extend the Canada Highways Act of 1919 and its amendments would require the same procedure-that is, a recommendation of the crown and a resolution. So with the Trans-Canada Highway Act. For these reasons, I find that the bill which is proffered by the hon. member is one which cannot be introduced by a private member.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to take some small part in this debate at this particular time. I may say that I have been waiting for some time and have been listening to the hon. members who have made their contributions from the ranks of the official opposition. I must say that I have been bitterly disappointed. The hon. gentlemen were apparently champing at the bit to get on with this debate on the economic affairs of the nation. One would have thought that they would unleash destructive critical power with regard to the ways in which this country has been governed and with respect to economics during the past several months. However, this has not been the case. Outside of a variety of pompous political platitudes and whining and whimpering about such things as getting the nation going again, imaginative thinking, dynamic growth and so on, there has not been anything of substance. Moreover, Mr. Chairman, I fail to see how there could be.
The Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Labour and others from time to time since this session started have placed on Hansard statistical information with regard to all the various indices and records which I think constitute the best possible indication of the fact that this country has made, is making and will continue to make substantial progress in such things as the gross national product, employment, sales, savings, and foreign trade. It is not necessary for me to gild the lily and to put this information before the committee again. It is there on record and is available for those who are interested and will seek it out. What I propose to do is this, and I think I do it for the reason that there are times when we who come to Ottawa become institutionalized. Sometimes, from this point of view, looking back at the rest of the country is like looking through a telescope from the wrong end. It is necessary to go back to our people and to the areas from which we come. The legislation we pass here and the measures we adopt are to be considered from the viewpoint of the impact they make on these people who include farmers, small businessmen, workers and professional people. How have these people fared as a result of the measures

which this government has taken? I am naturally far more familiar with the area from which I come than I am with any other area. This is one of the 265 cross sections of this country. This is why I propose to deal briefly and simply with the impact which has been made on the people of the country from which I come by the proposals and the legislation of this government.
One of the things I was primarily concerned in for some years and in which the people in my area were tremendously interested was the construction of a great national project in the form of a railway through the Peace river area into the Northwest Territories terminating at Pine Point and at Great Slave lake. Last fall this measure was passed. I should like briefly to recount to the members of the committee what has been the effect of the action taken as a result of this legislation. I should like to read and to put on the record a news item appearing in the Edmonton Journal. I am sure hon. members opposite will not be prepared to question articles appearing in the Edmonton Journal. Under date of August 22, 1962, the following article appeared in that paper under the byline of Rod Hayter, an experienced journalist with a knowledge of northern affairs who had made a careful on the spot survey of this railway and the extent to which it had progressed. The headline is "Great Slave Lake Railway Will Spur Exciting Northern Development" and the article reads in part as follows:
The Great Slave lake railway will be one of the most important small railways ever built.
The line will be another phase of Canadian history ranking in importance with such projects as the all Canadian natural gas pipe line and the opening of the ore fields in Quebec and Labrador.
Since that time what has happened? Since last fall 180 miles of right of way have been cut out. Contracts have been let for another 180 miles. On the first 180 miles contracts have been let and a large part of the actual grading has been completed. Track laying commenced last August. I have not the most up to date report but at this time I believe the track will have progressed to a point approximately 45 miles from railhead. The C.N.R. authorities have indicated that this line will have been pushed to a distance of approximately 73 miles by later this fall. This will mean, Mr. Chairman, that 8,000 to 10,000 farmers living in an area extending for 50 miles around the line, who have waited for many years for an opportunity to market their commodities, will have a chance to haul their grain to communities and towns much closer to where their farms are.
All this has meant the expenditure of millions of dollars. Thousands of jobs have been created and given to people not only

from our part of the country but from all sections of Canada, from other parts of Alberta, from British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and eastern Canada. All during the course of this winter hundreds of men will continue to be employed in cutting out the right of way and building bridges.
But there are collateral benefits. Naturally the construction of a great national project of this kind must necessarily involve the expenditure of large sums of money; but our point has always been, and this was the attitude taken by the government in promoting this project, that this would result in generating far more than the actual work involved in the building of the railroad. This has proven to be the case. I refer to another news item which appeared in the Edmonton Journal of the same date. It is a brief item which states that Mr. Jewett, the president of Pine Point Mines Limited, was reported as having said that Pine Point construction would start next summer. That is the summer of 1963. This construction is being carried on pursuant to the agreement worked out and placed on record at the time the legislation was passed last fall. What is involved in the beginning of the construction of the Pine Point mine? This was put on record by the Minister of Transport when, in speaking on second reading of the bill to provide for the construction of a line of railway to Great Slave lake, he said, as found on page 8503 of Hansard for September 18, 1961:
Construction of the railway line will bring about major new construction projects, namely, a $21 million mining camp at Pine Point; $16 million expansion of the plant of Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, at Trail, B.C.; a $2 million community development at Pine Point-
That is a total of approximately $40 million. But there are other things, Mr. Chairman. In our part of the country we have benefited from many aspects of the programs and legislation of the government but in particular from three major policies which, like three streams, have met and merged and flowed over the country like a great river at flood in the spring, bringing tremendous benefits, enriching the land and conferring great and substantial benefits upon the people. I refer to the programs with relation to agriculture, northern development and transportation.
I have talked about the railway and have said that it is proposed to reach a point some 70 miles from railhead this year. Now, if I may, I should like to deal with agriculture. I have a news item here taken from the Peace River Record-Gazette of August 2 last. This is a local newspaper published in my constituency. These newspapers are factual, non-partisan, independent and report things as they see them, a practice which might well
Ways and Means
commend itself to other journalists. The news item is headed, "Plan Four Elevators at Manning", and reads in part as follows:
A representative of the United Grain Growers Limited in Peace River said Tuesday that four elevator firms including U.G.G. will be placing elevators in the town of Manning starting this summer and expecting to be finished in October. The three other firms will be building new elevators; U.G.G. is moving one from Grimshaw.
The article goes on to say that the elevators will have a total capacity of half a million bushels and will cost approximately a third of a million dollars to build. In the Grande Prairie Herald-Tribune of August 7 last, another newspaper published in my constituency, there is an article headed, "North Land Rush Biggest Since War", and reading in part as follows:
In the biggest homestead rush since pioneer days, the Peace River country has caught the fancy of land seekers from across western Canada. Reviewing the cascade of inquiries about holdings in the north, district lands supervisor Tom Gorman said Tuesday morning in Grande Prairie the activity has topped even the busy post-war period of 1946 and 1947 .. .
Officials said an average of 60 to 70 persons daily had been calling at the office.
The office in Grande Prairie is one of two land offices, the other one being in the town of Peace River. These articles bear out the observations I have made personally, which indicate that from all over Canada and the United States 150 to 200 people a day have been coming into our region seeking to take up land and discover for themselves the benefits which this government has been conferring on the farmers, something which did not exist for a long time. I did some farming myself before I came to Ottawa but I found that under the previous administration it took a fairly good law practice to keep up a farm in those days.
I should also like to refer to an editorial in the Herald-Tribune of October 16 and I do so because I have heard from hon. members opposite a lot of doom and gloom about agriculture and farming and I think there should be an answer. The editorial is headed, "The Real Key To The Future", and reads as follows:
As the last of the harvest comes in and autumn winds riffle through the tinted bush, vast areas of "the Peace" are stretching to wakefulness after generations of slumber. A new symphony of sound is echoing in huge tracts of bush-covered land stitched to long settled parts of the Peace river country . .. The rush which began picking up steam early this year shows no sign of tapering off. By the end of the year, up to half a million acres of new potential farmland may have been taken up.
It is not only the settlement of the land, Mr. Chairman. For many years we found it difficult to secure any form of assistance for the farmers of that area by way of farm

Ways and Means
loans. My best estimate would be that in all the 22 years during which hon. gentlemen opposite held control of the reins of government less than $100,000 was lent to farmers for the purpose of generating and building up their productive capacity. I have a news item here from the Herald-Tribune of October 12 which is headed, "$2.6 Million Loan Tally Bolsters Farms In North". So we have $2,600,000 by the middle of September this year, $2,500,000 last year and about $1,500,000 for the year before, or almost $7 million in less than three years compared with $100,000 in the preceding 22 years. This has had additional benefits, Mr. Chairman. As the result of the inflow of people to our area, as a result of the fact farmers have been able to improve their holdings to increase their productive capacity, it has been estimated by those who know that holdings of approximately 2 million acres now under cultivation in the Peace River area have been increased in value by no less than $10 an acre for the entire acreage. This would mean to the farmers of the Peace River area about $20 million.
Now, I leave agriculture to deal with lumber. We have a diversified economy in that area. Under date of September 28, 1962, I notice an article in the Herald-Tribune headed, "Lumbermen Plan Big Winter Cut". The article reads, in part:
Plans for a bigger-than-ever timber cut in the Grande Prairie area were unveiled this week by the city's major lumber and plywood producers.
One company alone is planning to cut about 50 million board feet for lumber and plywood purposes. This will be duplicated in all three forestry districts of the entire area. As an aside, Mr. Chairman, it may be of interest for hon. members to know that in discussing this matter with those who are engaged in the lumbering business, I found they were most pleased with the devaluation of the dollar by the government, and suggested this would mean $5 or $6 extra per thousand board feet in their pockets.
Then, I should like to deal with gas and oil. I have here a news report from the Record-Gazette which has the following headline, "Shell Plans to Build Gas Plant at Worsley". This refers to the construction of a pipe line and gas processing plant in the Worsley district which will involve the expenditure of millions of dollars.
It is not necessary to stop there. All this activity and increase in population in the urban communities and farming areas has had a marked effect. The Herald-Tribune of October 5 carries a heading, "Building Strides Near $4 Million". This one community, according to the article, will have a building

construction program involving an expenditure of $400,000. The same situation prevails in other communities. It has been estimated, Mr. Chairman, that there will be no less than $12 million to $15 million spent in new housing, new plants and other construction in the urban communities of this constituency of less than 80,000 people.
The Herald-Tribune of October 5 carries an article to the effect that the area will have its first television programs within two weeks. This means that 75,000 or 80,000 people will, by the first week in November, enjoy the same opportunities and facilities as other Canadians, and will be able to tune in for the first time to television. This has involved an expenditure of several millions of dollars, not only in the construction of the television facilities but in the sale of new television sets and the construction of the microwave lines for carrying programs.
I go on from there, Mr. Chairman. This is something which will be of interest to hon. members opposite. The Grande Prairie Herald-Tribune has this headline, "Jobless Total Tumbles". The article reads in part:
Spurred on by a healthy construction pace during September, unemployment has dropped to the lowest ebb in two years in the Peace River district, it was noted this week.
"The job-seeker list we have is the lowest since the office opened," said national employment service manager ..
This comment applies to every part of the country. Now, Mr. Chairman, I put all this on the record because I have heard hon. gentlemen opposite talking about spurring on the economy, getting Canada moving again. I should like to call to their attention the fact that in September of last year we brought before the house a bill for the construction of the railway needed in the Great Slave area. One would have thought that hon. gentlemen opposite would have been the first to do all that they could to see this measure become law. However, after putting as many roadblocks as they possibly could in the way of the bill, on third reading they moved a motion for a six months' hoist. This would, in effect, have killed the bill. When the house divided on the motion for third reading, the official opposition voted against it.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if they had had their way very little of this tremendous expansion which took place in my constituency, and of which I have presented convincing evidence, would have been brought about. I would suggest to hon. gentlemen opposite that the noise they have been making hides a very weak case. I was trying to think of an apt term which described their performance during the course of this debate, and my mind turned back to a very funny movie I saw once entitled, "The Mouse that Roared".

In my opinion, nothing else could better describe the actions and words of hon. members opposite.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that other hon. members, if they had the opportunity and the time, could present an equally good record to this committee. This proves that, far from what has been suggested by hon. members opposite, the economic policies of this government have been sound, have been effective and have resulted in a substantial increase in the standard of living of the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, on the first occasion on which I speak in this house, I should like to congratulate you on your appointment as chairman. In the past, the people of York North have entrusted their parliamentary representation to notable Canadians. The history of the constituency is marked by men who well understood the principles of representative and responsible government. It was in York North that William Lyon Mackenzie began his famous march on Toronto to upset the family compact. It was York North which later elected Mackenzie's grandson, Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, to represent the constituency, when he was Prime Minister of Canada. It was York North which sent to parliament Mr. King's early and great political mentor Sir William Mul-ock, and Sir Allan Aylesworth. It fell to Sir William's son, the Hon. "Bill" Mulock to follow in his father's cabinet footsteps. I shall not refer to all of my predecessors, but I should like to mention Mr. Jack Smith who represented the riding so well and so effectively. He was very much in the great tradition of York North. Nor do I want to let this occasion pass without referring to my immediate predecessor Mr. Cecil "Tiny" Cathers. He was, and remains a fine gentleman and a generous opponent.
Our riding of York North is a miniature of Ontario. We have in York North really the extension of the great metropolitan area of Toronto. We are urban, suburban, exurban, rural and resort country. We have large market towns and small villages. Almost nowhere has the population increased as rapidly as in the southern part of our constituency. Once our riding was primarily a rural riding with a few notable and historic towns such as Richmond Hill, Newmarket, Aurora, Markham and Sutton. These towns remain but they have grown much larger. They are important suburban communities. One of the problems that has arisen in our riding is that of commuting. A great number of our people in the riding of York North travel 50 miles each day to work. Many of these people work in Toronto and the surrounding area. Additionally, a very large
Ways and Means
proportion of our people work in industry and in small business within the borders of our constituency.
On a broader plane, Mr. Chairman, I would like to say that a social revolution is occurring in our time and I want to pay particular attention to this social revolution as it affects our economy and as our economy affects it. I refer to York North because I think it is significant. It is directly affected by the modern movements of which I have spoken. It is symptomatic of a changing North America and the effects of this change on all governments are exceedingly important. Governments, however, and legislatures have been slow to realize and recognize the importance of this change that has come about after 30 years of development. A mobile society has been created in our suburbs and our exurbs, but it has done far more than that; it has changed the internal character of our older rural areas, and as a result what we have now are centralized merchandising areas that are made possible by the ease of automobile transportation. This has altered the pattern of our economy and also of our whole society. This has given us new problems and these problems have been ignored. If we continue to ignore them we are going to be faced with a very unsound economic future.
Living has not only changed as far as areas are concerned; it has changed as far as buying habits and distribution are concerned, with regard to work and to recreation. We no longer today have arbitrary borders between cities and country, or between one community and another. People move from one jurisdiction to another for work, education, recreation, buying and selling. The facilities of one area are often today used by the residents of adjacent communities as much as by their own residents. And taxation is very much affected by all this. The distribution of municipal, provincial and federal revenues is very much involved, and yet very little has been done to study the character of this change in our social economy, let alone to try to find any permanent solutions that this situation has created.
In its very nature this kind of mobile society has forced more attention from federal governments and has added national responsibilities even though centralization may be resisted. Yet as this happens, there is a real paradox in our Canadian way of life. While federal government more than ever exerts direct control of our affairs, these functions are being thrown back to municipal and provincial interests. Federal government has got so big or so complex that it has gone beyond the ordinary man's comprehension and

Ways and Means
world affairs, as far as he is concerned, are now occupying the federal government's deliberations.
I think we are significantly aware in the last few days, with the Cuban crisis, just how this situation has arisen. We should realize, from this example, that the average taxpayer fears, most unfortunately, that it is all too big for him to grapple with. As a result he often turns to things that are closer to him and things that he is capable of changing. Yet, again the paradox. Provincial and municipal authorities are in turn forced to seek more attention from their central government. This places a new and heavy burden on the members of parliament. It becomes their duty and responsibility to maintain a close awareness of what their government is doing, and to keep in touch with world affairs and keep their constituents constantly aware of what is happening.
As I say, people are more and more faced with the problems that they were not faced with previously. Yet we are trying to operate today under a method and system of government that existed a century ago. I, like so many people-and I think this is indicative, after the last election-now entering public life for the first time have been attempting to find some solution to these problems. I for one suggest that these solutions are hard to find because, as I said earlier, we have learned so very little about our real situation and its origins and ramifications.
Some things we do know about our country. We know that the small businessman and the farmer is under ever increasing pressure from taxes, overhead costs, competition from chain stores and massive discount houses, and from the difficulty of raising operating capital and from high interest rates. We know also that smaller industries are under similar restraints, but that additionally they are affected directly by the national trade policies of our government. I suggest that these people are seriously in need of help which they, as individuals, cannot provide by way of research and trade information but which their taxes should provide through government agencies. I suggest that we, as Canadians, should look closely at other countries that have been successful in this sphere.
I refer to the October 22 issue of the V.S. News and World Report, which refers to the tremendous growth of Japan's industries. Many think one of the big reasons for Japan's success is her government's policy toward business. The government, through an economic planning agency, the bank of Japan, and other agencies, sets the course and pace for economic growth. Then it leaves the job to private enterprise. It is a business-minded government, and national budgets usually

show a surplus. If there is a deficit, it is small. Private investment outruns government investment three to one. I am very much of the opinion that we have been resting on our oars, so far as international trade expansion is concerned. I am of the firm belief that:	(1) Export trade can only be
expanded by an intelligent appraisal of our national resources to evaluate to what extent we can increase the Canadian labour content in products of these materials. (2) Secondary and service industries along with labour must look to world prices rather than charge what the traffic will bear in their pricing policies. (3) We should recognize that there is going to be a reduction in our Canadian tariffs and prepare now for competition so that our own domestic markets will not be completely disrupted. (4) We should take our products to the potential buyer. I doubt very much-an hon. member has mentioned mice-that if we were to build a better mousetrap today the world would beat a path to our door. But I do feel that in each of our potential trade areas we should establish a showcase of Canada's manufactured goods, free of charge to the exhibitor, on a revolving schedule, so that we could show our manufactured products in the country in which we choose to sell them. (5) We should analyse carefully and professionally the potential markets and then bring products that are manufactured in other countries to Canadian manufacturers and encourage them to produce them in this country for export. I am also of the opinion that at the present time we are exporting products we make for our own industries and population here, and we therefore must look to and accept products from other countries, analyse them here, and then produce them for export only. We should have tax credits and incentives to encourage our industry to produce products that will sell at competitive world prices.
In a debate such as this we might contrast the banking system in the United States which, to a large extent, operates on a local level and is often family owned in small areas, with our present banking system in Canada which is operated on the branch system. There is something to be said for the banking system in the United States where the personnel of banks remain reasonably permanent in any one area, and where the prosperity of a bank in a particular community depends on the prosperity of the community and on the bank's ability to lend money in that community. We should perhaps look for greater integration of banks in Canada with the community.
Restrictions on lending have the unfortunate effect of creating the cycle they attempt to avoid by holding down business activity at a time when the country is sorely in need of

business expansion. Mr. Fraser Robertson, in his column on the financial page of the Globe and Mail suggested that money is tight or easy by degree. He went on to say that without high interest rates money for investment would be even scarcer than it has been, and said free marketing and free trade go along with a free money movement. This may be so but it is hard to find any flow of easy money in Canada today. Mr. Robertson holds that we must win confidence by presenting prospectuses for our future more attractive than those presented by developers of other areas, so that those who control money will invest it in our country. I suggest that he is talking about confidence generated by the government in this context; but over the period which the Conservative government has been in office any person in business has had to look very hard to find stability in Canada's financial situation.
There are various ways to restore confidence in our country. There is room for expansion of the industrial development bank, and I also suggest that a ministry of industry and small business be established. This is important, so that we can set up research facilities and provide assistance to keep this part of our economy moving ahead. Borrowing is not enough. Money does not cure all problems. The small businessman or farmer needs the guidance and experience of trained personnel.
I suggest that the area of small business is not in good order today, and that is not entirely the fault of the businessmen themselves. They are being trapped by broader things. With such a department the government would be in a position to provide some focus in this field. In saying this I am fully aware of the danger of intrusion by government into business and private enterprise, but I do not suggest that it is a question of planning or not planning. That really is the doctrine of the '20's and '30's. Since then we have learned a great deal about planning, and we know that the right kind of planning is essential for the growth of the country.
I am not so interested in total or centralized planning which is done too far from the source of the social and business conditions *concerned. I am thinking of long term assistance and incentive to regional planning for the sensible and prudent use of available resources. It is interesting to note in this context that the only country behind the iron curtain which has no food problem is Poland. The reason it does not have this problem, which is one shared by Russia, Czechoslovakia and the Balkan countries, is that planning is done for these other countries from Moscow, but planning for Poland is done from Warsaw. The Poles refused to deliver from collectivised farms and when the communists found that
Ways and Means
the Polish farmers simply would not deliver, they modified their schemes and permitted a return to private farming.
We should also consider the worrisome question of price maintenance. Discounting and price slashing have made it almost impossible for the small businessman to make a profit, let alone survive in business or industry. I realize that talk of price maintenance to some extent smacks of combines, and that combines are not popular. However, there must be a middle way, a sensible compromise which allows for reasonable floors under prices and which prevents the dog-eat-dog tactics which marked big business in the United States in the days of the Vanderbilts and the Morgans.
The fight today is between powerful concerns in the consumer goods field competing against local stores in the same field. I am not advocating control, but socially we need small business and industry, for many reasons. First of all, there is local investment and close concern with the community. Then there is the contribution of taxation and the matter of leadership and support given to local areas by small businessmen and industrialists. There is also the provision of varied employment, and there is the convenience.
I suggest that what we and our economists have been doing is looking at only one side of the issue, the economic side. We have thought very little about the social cost to our communities, through our failure to help the small businessman and farmer meet the tremendous obstacles facing them at present.
All business, in the broader sense, is affected because Canada in recent years stopped expanding. This was not necessary and it should not have happened. European countries, which we were reluctant to recognize, have done things we are astonished at today. France, even in face of the tremendous crisis in Algeria and general political turmoil, kept its economy expanding at a healthy rate. This was done by a system of federal planning which co-ordinated the policies of government, business and labour. This is the kind of function I have in mind when I speak of planning and co-ordination with the assistance of a special government department of industry and small business.
In the past we have allowed ourselves to be taken in by the extremist positions of the far-rightists and the far-leftists. We have listened to the cries of the socialist party in this country as it preached doctrines that were tried and thrown out by the British a generation ago, and by Europeans more recently. We have seen them perpetuate an antiquated class war between labour and management, or more accurately between

Ways and Means
labour and capital because management today is not necessarily capital and management does not often imply ownership.
Of course the rights of labour exist and must be respected as much as the rights of capital and management. Anyone who would dispute this is living in a different era. If there is no partnership between them, then business and industry cannot compete in world markets, but just as the rights of labour must be respected so must the rights of those who provide management and capital. Not only is there room for co-operation, but cooperation is essential.
Anyone who is up to date in his economic and social thinking knows that extremists of either capital or labour, who attempt to maintain conditions and attitudes that were prevalent 30 years ago, are beyond help. Management, labour and capital have to come together and work out their problems together. This has been done in Europe, in countries such as Germany, France, Belgium, Switzerland, and more increasingly in Italy. As an interesting example, new ideas in the field of co-operation have made us here in Canada appear a generation behind the times. Many of the ideas we are tentatively exploring have been accepted in full body as practical measures in these countries, and it is about time we modernized our ideas here in Canada.
There is one more subject that I would like to mention, and only briefly because I am not a sufficiently informed authority in the field to talk about it at any length, and that is taxation. I am quite convinced that the small businessman has been made to bear an unfair and overweighted burden of taxation. This is one of the reasons his survival is so difficult. Surely the time has come when federal, provincial and municipal authorities must get together and try to work some sense into this problem. The old fears of stepping on one another's toes are antiquated, and a new co-operation must be found here, just as between capital, labour and management in private business and industry-established in the face of harsh realities. A Professor William M. Partlan of Fordham college in New York city offers a scheme which I think is interesting in connection with tax cuts. Some people today think we should have higher taxes, but this eminent teacher puts forward some very strong arguments to show how, properly handled, income tax cuts could enliven the economy and increase national spending.
Europe has over the past years known what we consider full employment. Apart from wartime, Canada has never experienced it. Indispensable to full employment is a continuing growth in economic development.
[Mr. Addison.l
Even in a country such as the United States* which, of course, Mr. Partlan is mainly concerned about, there is a great distance between full employment and what exists now. So here, in Canada, we have not only to catch up from a long way behind but we have to induce a much faster growth, once we have come level with what we could consider a minimum position for ordinary prosperity. Tax policy at the federal level has much to do with this. As I have said, the right kind of tax cuts would go a long way to spurring such development.
The purpose of income tax cutting should be to increase purchasing and saving power among the masses of the people. Cuts at high level incomes do little to affect this, and cutting taxes at the top income levels adds very little to the savings and spending of our country. Let us refer to family spending units and consider them with regard to taxation rather than as individuals. Normally, only one or two individuals in a family are what we consider wage earners, but the family outgoings are handled by several people. The wage earner ordinarily does not support himself only; he supports his whole family. It is true that exemptions take this into account, but the tax structure today makes personal income tax primarily a personal tax. Partlan's idea is that the federal income tax should be based on family rather than personal income, and he holds that a proper cut would necessarily be a personal income tax cut with a very careful estimate of the impact of the cut on family spending. Using his own country's statistics he shows that the middle 50 per cent of all income tax returns in the United States is in the disposable income area between $2,085 and $6,580. This is where most of the income taxes come from. He shows that this group takes in about 30 million families, perhaps 120 million people, or nearly two thirds of the entire population of the United States. To state it simply, then: for almost all people in the medium income tax brackets, a progressive income tax rate means nothing, since there is little progress in their income; and when there is, family extensions and new requirements take it up.
There is, therefore, a group of the population that pays a basic rate, and a cut in such a rate would affect family and national spending as well as potential savings, almost, I would suggest, to the full extent of the tax cuts. This would stimulate economic growth by augmenting purchasing power in his own country of the United States, of two thirds or more of all the nation's family units who would reasonably be expected to spend or to save all of the additional take home pay.
The belief that all of the money left for family spending by an income tax cut would

go immediately into consumer goods and services is reasonable. Most families are far from having what they reasonably desire, other than the necessities of life. Professor Partlan holds that even a 1 or 2 per cent increase in his nation's total consumer expenditures would be enough to accelerate investment and stimulate economic growth. But he agrees that it would be most difficult to determine what the size of the cut should be. However, he maintains that the higher level of spending from such a cut would probably offset the government's loss in revenue resulting from this cut. Certainly any effort to raise spending, increase demand, and consequently production, is a worth-while one.
In particular, Canada might well think about this scheme, since we have so many smaller industries and so much small business which would benefit by consumer spending directly. It is family spending units which do most to energize the economy by their reasonable requirements. Being realistic, we in Canada certainly know large numbers of families are far from having the purchasing power which a modern industrialized society should give them. There are many thousands of families in urgent need, and some in extreme need, of things which people in higher income groups take for granted as necessities. There is no question but that the additional money allowed by alteration of income tax would go quickly to useful purposes. It would also have a lasting and important benefit to our total economy if we tried to provide frugal comfort for all our people.

Mr. Chairman, before making a contribution to this debate, I want to set the record straight as regards a statement, an allegation, made in an editorial of the October issue of the magazine the Legionary, I find the following about myself.
This politician recently elected to parliament-
What is wrong with that?

-is supposed to have said at a press conference:
I am still quoting:
I have just taken the most shameful oath in my life, I just swore allegiance to Her Majesty the Queen of England.
Now, Mr. Chairman, that statement is an utter falsehood. I never uttered any such statement. I have never given any press conference in the course of which I stated anything of the sort.
Ways and Means
If the reporter or the editorial writer who took it upon himself to make that accusation is a responsible man, I ask him, from the floor of the house, to publish an honest retraction in the same newspaper.
However there is nothing surprising in the attitude of reporters and editorial writers toward Social Credit. The reason is that we have been bothering them pretty much for many years. They always try to represent us in a wrong light, in a false light. They put in our mouths words that we do not say in order to be later in a better position to raise objections to their own creations or fancies.
Mr. Chairman, we could not care less about what those newsmen write-and I told them so many times-whether it is favourable or unfavourable to us, for six months or a year, since on television we can easily reply to them in 15 minutes and settle accounts with them.
Mr. Chairman, in regard to the revised estimates where the Minister of Finance announces cuts of the order of $227 million, under the pretence that we must live up to our international commitments, that we must even out the unfavourable balance of our trade or even make it favourable. I do not think that that is the way towards acceptable prosperity, a true prosperity for Canada.
A reduction of $227 million was made, $18,200,000 for public works, $6,400,000 previously allocated to agriculture and other departments, so that they amount to a total of $227 million.
They are proud of those reductions from the Fleming budget of last February or March, in order to ensure the economic stability of the country; they claim that those reductions would stabilize the economy to the advantage of the country. It is the opposite that will happen.
When we reduce the estimates of such departments as public works, agriculture, colonization and others in the country, we deprive them of their means of existence, we stop them from carrying on their operations and normal development.
Thus, we give rise to more unemployment, we increase the number of unemployed in Canada.
Let us vote against.
Everyone is in favour of-
Yours is a morganatic marriage.

Wait and see.

Ways and Means
Mr. Chairman, what I and the Canadian people find astonishing is that Canada's economic activity is being restricted by a cut in the budget expenditures, while the Minister of Finance, in the newspapers, on the radio and in the house, talks about what he calls a tremendous success.
The government has announced that its deficit will be $175 million less than what was forecast last February or March, but it still remains that the deficit amounts to $540 million.
A few days ago, the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) stated that the interest on the national debt alone is higher than the deficit. Yet, instead of penalizing those who charge us interest for a fictitious debt, make-believe credit, it is the Canadian people, men, women and children who are penalized. Let us cut their supplies but let us keep on paying interest at the rate of $800 million a year. Those $800 million are sacred. Nobody questions that. No austerity program is being introduced for Canada's financiers.
An austerity program for the human being in Canada is proposed to us. Well, we of the Social Credit party, are of the opinion that when it is necessary to apply an austerity program in this Canada of ours we should apply it first to finance and free the country so that we will have prosperity for Canadians.
Mr. Chairman, the important cuts announced in the revised estimates will result in still greater hardship in Canada.
One need not have gone to college, be a lawyer or a scientist or an economist to understand that international communism- or even national communism-has its cradle in cases of national hardship. As long as misery will prevail within abundance-and I can see that the Minister of Finance is at his desk-as long as we shall accept misery to exist within abundance, all such cases of hardship will be as so many dynamite sticks inside our Canadian social structure, which someday the communists will ignite.
This afternoon, I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) speak about the danger which the grave Cuban crisis represents for us, this crisis which could easily start a nuclear war tomorrow, or the day after. He told us to be ready.
Mr. Chairman, the moment war comes, be it tonight, tomorrow or the day after,

I am convinced the financial question will be quickly solved in Canada to enable us to wage war and defend our country.
But when Canada has 500,000 unemployed, human beings, our fellow Canadians, our electors, people in our constituencies, living in dire poverty, this is not considered an emergency which calls for an immediate meeting to deal with their cases and seek to alleviate their misery. They are cast aside, they are promised the moon, they are told to be patient, they are allowed to exist by means of unemployment insurance benefits, but to give them a Canadian system, an economic system through which each one of them could develop freely, no thought is given to that.
On this side of the house, hon. members rather share the views of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), and like him, they attack Social Credit without knowing what it is all about. Other hon. members reflect upon the Social Credit philosophy and say we will cause inflation. And some newspapers such as the Toronto Telegraph or the Toronto daily Star do the same. After my recent visit to the Toronto junior board of trade and to the Montreal Canadian Club- where we had 1,300 people at a luncheon talk-I had the pleasure of meeting many businessmen, small merchants and professionals of all categories, who live in anxiety in Canada.
Everybody is concerned-small businessmen, professionals, labourers, in short everybody is in doubt in Canada. To this economical and financial anxiety that we know at present, anxiety about a war, a war possible within a few weeks, is now being added.

Inflation, Mr. Chairman, is what comes when we have money on hand and there is not enough production to guarantee that money. When there is no production and there is money, that is where you have inflation.
Today, it is the opposite. I wish they would stop raising the cry of inflation when deflation is what we have in Canada, because people do not have enough money to buy all the different kinds of products we have in this country.

If you ever saw a man in the moon, he is the one. He does not need Khrushchev to send him up because he is there already. (Text):

Social Credit failed in Canada when our supreme court repudiated all the laws passed in Alberta in 1937-39, 1941, 1944, 1947. For a group of sensible men of reasonably good education to listen to Mr. Caouette and be carried away by his oratory to the point of admiration is incredible ... We can find about the same thing in the Toronto daily Star:

I do not tell him either what is the ration of displacement of the piston within the engine.
Mr. Chairman, the member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville drives a car, but I would bet my best shirt that he knows absolutely nothing about a car engine, but yet he drives the car.

For 22 years we have used a Liberal engine in Canada, and that is why we have been in the ditch ever since. Here is part of the study made by that economist on the national dividend advocated by Social Credit to supplement the purchasing power, which would permit the purchase of actual goods and actual services existing in Canada.
The national dividend implies the monetization of the new production, carried out by the federal treasury, through the Bank of Canada, so that the additional production may be represented by an additional financial credit made available to the people. In other words, goods are actually available for the dividend and it is easy to create the financial credit required for distribution thereof.
The real answer to the unemployment problem is therefore to create a constant demand for goods by making the money available to consumers-[DOT]
Everybody admits that. When consumers have money, business is good; when consumers have no money, business is slow and everything may even come to a standstill in the country.
-either under the form of salaries or of dividends so that full employement will exist as long as there is an unsatisfied demand for goods.

The hon. members who attack the Social Credit doctrine should first of all study Social Credit instead of making it up.

Neither the Liberals nor the Conservatives have found any solution to that problem, but when we suggest a solution, right away an attempt is made to ridicule Social Credit.
Some people prefer solutions like those offered by Maurice Lamontagne, chief economist of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec and in Canada.
That is true.

So, the proposed remedy, which will perhaps be applied after the war, is much less a result than a start, opening as it does the way to two absolutely contrary systems-capitalist dictatorship and socialism-
He does not say "socialist dictatorship", but "socialism".
But, Mr. Chairman, what is socialism? For the information of those who do not know its definition, I would suggest they refer to the "Concise Oxford Dictionary", in which socialism is defined as follows:
(Text):
Principle that individual freedom should be completely subordinated to interests of community, with any deductions that may be correctly or incorrectly drawn from it, e.g. substitution of cooperative for competitive production, national ownership of land and capital, state distribution of produce, free education and feeding of children and abolition of inheritance.

The solution of the economist who is preeminently a Liberal, is to oppose capitalism to socialism, instead of correcting capitalism.
Therefore, in one way or another, under the Liberals we are sure to turn more and more to socialism in this country and in our respective provinces.

Mr. Chairman, in this morning's Le Devoir, there is signed by Mr. P. H. Lavallee, an engineer, a concise and simple study of Social Credit which means something. This is what Mr. Lavallee says:
It has always been objected that such a measure is causing inflation-as if there were no middle road between a chronic lack of purchasing power and inflation.

(Text):
Before dealing with the budget resolutions which are now before the committee, I should like to comment briefly on one or two other subjects. First I want to express my great pleasure on the election of Mr. T. C. Douglas on Monday of this week. I join my colleagues in thanking the people of Burnaby-Coquitlam for the very solid support given to the federal leader of our party. Burnaby has been supporting the C.C.F. and the New Democratic party since 1933, when the late Ernest E. Winch, the father of the hon. member for Vancouver East, was first elected to the legislature of British Columbia by the people of Burnaby. He remained as member for Burnaby until his death in 1957.
(Translation):
Take your dictionary, sir.
(Text):
Mr. Chairman, I was saying that Mr. Winch, the father of the hon. member for Vancouver East, was a pioneer in the field of social reform in British Columbia. As a result of Mr. Winch's persistence very great changes were made in the treatment of the mentally ill in our province. As a result of his efforts, many changes were made in our penal institutions. He pioneered in the field of providing housing for senior citizens, and the first home of its type in Canada was, I believe, established in Burnaby by the New Vista society, which was founded by Mr. Winch. Since his death he has been succeeded by other members of our party, and in the legislature of British Columbia there are now two members from Burnaby representing the New Democratic party, Mr. Gordon Dowding and Mr. Cedric Cox. The riding of Burnaby-Coquitlam came into existence in 1953. In that year Mr. Erhart Regier was elected. He was re-elected in 1957, 1958 and 1962. Certainly my colleagues and I appreciate the part Mr. Regier has played in the recent by-election victory in Burnaby-Coquitlam.
My own riding of Burnaby-Richmond tried and discarded in turn all of the other three parties, and in June of 1962 they did the New Democratic party and myself the honour of supporting us. I trust this happy relationship will continue for many years to come.
Mr. Chairman, I want to make just a few points on the international situation as it relates to Cuba. First, I noted the other evening that the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona rose in what seemed to be a very hostile atmosphere and made some dissenting remarks about the Cuban situation. I
Ways and Means
certainly admire his courage for doing that in the particular situation. There is one aspect of the Cuban situation, the international situation, upon which I think some comment is necessary. We understand there are some members of the government who want to equip our armed forces with nuclear weapons. There is a danger that a tense international situation such as exists now, and may well exist in the near future, may be the occasion for attempting to change government policy regarding nuclear weapons for the Canadian forces.
There appears to be no doubt that there are missile bases in Cuba, but I do not know that we can say for sure that these bases are equipped with nuclear weapons. However, if it is later proven that this is the case, I think this fact proves that the spread of nuclear weapons increases the danger of war. We have said many times before that every addition to the nuclear club endangers peace, and we are more than ever convinced that this is so. I was pleased this afternoon when the Leader of the Opposition stated that he too was concerned about the spread of the nuclear weapons club. I took this to mean that he is opposed to Canada having nuclear weapons. I am very glad he made that statement, because I have been disturbed by the tone of questions on matters of defence and external affairs coming from the Liberal benches during the past week. They were beginning to sound like a war party beginning to change its policy on this matter, and I am very glad the leader of the party has put that matter straight.
What about what they said during the election campaign?

I do not know about during the election campaign. They just did not seem to know what Liberal policy was on this particular matter. To speak particularly of budget matters and the revised estimates which have been placed before the house, I wish to refer to the estimates of two departments in particular, the Department of Public Works and the Department of Labour, and especially the winter works program. I was very sorry to see a reduction of approximately $18 million in the estimates of the Department of Public Works. Here I do not complain of any reduction in my own riding. As far as I know, there was no estimate for it in the first place. However, in view of the number of unemployed throughout Canada, any reduction in public works spending does not make very much sense.
It would seem that Drs. Diefenbaker, Nowlan and McCutcheon and the other members of the Conservative clinic have looked at poor, sick Canada and have said, "We will

Ways and Means
cure him by starving him". As other hon. members have said, and as most economists have agreed, they have given the wrong prescriptions for the ills of this country. They should be deprived of their licences to practice. I would refer the Canadian people to the excellent clinic headed by Dr. Douglas.
I am pleased to note that the budget slashing has not affected the winter works program of the Department of Labour; at least, as far as I can tell. However, the amount of the government's contribution to the winter works program is only $12J million. This is a very small sum for a country the size of Canada. I want to concentrate on the winter works program for a few minutes, Mr. Chairman. The best that can be said for it is that it is better than no program at all. Some people have obtained work as a result of it, and municipalities have received some financial assistance from the federal and provincial governments.
At this point I think it is well to remind hon. members that the winter works program was suggested to the government by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities at a conference called by the Minister of Labour in July, 1958. I wish I could say that the government had initiated the program because it was concerned about aiding municipal development, but such was not the case. The government was faced with increasing unemployment and this was a measure which would help to reduce it a little.
Long before that time the C.C.F. party had been advocating a program of aid to municipalities. It did so for two reasons, the first being that it would provide employment. At this point I would remind hon. members that there was serious winter unemployment even in the wonderful Liberal years before 1957. The second, and equally important reason, was that federal financial aid would help the rapidly expanding urban areas to provide essential public services for their residents.
Those of us who have been in local government in recent years realize the extent of urban and metropolitan problems. Some hon. members may think that it is here in the House of Commons that all important decisions are made. However I suggest that those who serve on city councils are the first to grapple with the problems created by economic and technological change, and that they are carrying some of the most critical responsibilities for public policy in Canada.
Some of the problems are structural, that is they concern the type of government needed in heavily populated regions. The question of metro government amalgamation, or regional government, is one which will have to be settled by these municipalities in consultation with their respective provincial

governments. Here they do not need, nor do they ask for federal help; but whatever the type of local government, there still remains the need to pay for essential services. In this connection the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities has made many useful suggestions as to how the national government may assist in the solution of these problems.
It has suggested a municipal development bank, and here I shall quote from the federation's bulletin of December, 1961:
The primary tool of the new federal-provincial-municipal partnership in mobilizing capital would be a municipal development bank. In a special section of the brief, the federation states its case for such a bank in terms of both national and municipal needs which are summarized in the statement that the bank would be "a missing link
(1)	in upgrading municipal capital requirements to the equal status which they deserve with those of the federal and provincial governments;
(2)	in facilitating-for the purpose of assuring economic growth and stability-the constant review of the nation's need for capital expenditure; and
(3)	in implementing, to the advantage of the entire national economy, the policy of drawing to the utmost upon Canadian savings for our capital investment."
The importance of that proposal is this; in order to participate in the winter works program the municipalities have to borrow, and I suppose all hon. members know that the largest part of a winter works program is paid by the participating municipalities. In order to borrow they have to compete with the federal and provincial governments in the money markets. This means that they have to borrow at high interest rates, which show up in property taxes. They are in the same position as the person who cannot afford to take advantage of bargain prices.
The principle of integrated or co-operative borrowing has been accepted by the government in the national housing authority sewer legislation, and we ask that this principle be extended to other local works.
The federation has also suggested that the section of the National Housing Act which governs rural redevelopment, section 23, be amended to include non-residential properties. The federation recognizes, and my own experience confirms, that there are many depressed commercial areas in need of aid. When an area is seriously blighted it is necessary to look at the whole area, and not just the residential part of it. The need for redevelopment is obvious in many cities, and may I observe since coming down here a month ago that there is a great need for redevelopment in Ottawa and Hull.
There are many ways by which the federal government could provide employment and assist municipal governments to create good urban living areas. At this time I shall not

go into much detail, but for those hon. members who wish to be better informed on the subject I would refer them to the annual briefs of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities presented to the cabinet, and to a booklet entitled "There is work for Canadians in the improvement of our cities and towns."
I would add that this is all very productive work. The Minister of Finance seemed to suggest the other night that many types of public work projects were not productive. I do not believe that public works spending is the entire answer to all our economic problems, but it has a very definite place in any planning program to create economic growth. However I fear that a government bent on balancing the budget will not implement these useful and sensible proposals.
Perhaps the treasury benches should be reminded of President Kennedy's words to congress when he said "A stronger nation and economy requires more than a balanced budget. They require progress in those programs that spur our growth and fortify our strength." He went on to say "A strong America depends on its cities." I would paraphrase that and say a strong Canada depends on healthy cities. I look forward to the day when the cities of Canada, the places where over 85 per cent of the population live, will receive more federal assistance in creating healthy and pleasant environments for an expanding population.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Villeneuve gave us a very interesting presentation this evening, and in it he chose to say that you do not have to understand Social Credit in order to vote for it. In effect he said "Follow us blindly and there is every hope of a great economic future." I understand the hon. member is an automobile salesman and he certainly believes in the horseless carriage era, but I am sure that if there were something wrong with the automobile I was driving I would take it to his mechanic rather than to the dealer himself.
This afternoon the hon. member for Calgary South treated us to an interesting survey of the development of the oil and gas industry in Western Canada. Upon reflection I am sure he will admit that much of its development has been due to the great and vast pipe line projects that were undertaken during the Liberal administration. These included West-coast Transmission, Trans Mountain, Trans-Canada and the pipe line which terminated at Duluth and which was carried on later, I believe, to Sarnia. These were all developments under the former Liberal administration.
Ways and Means
I was very interested to listen this evening to the hon. member for Peace River, who pointed out the developments in that area due to the building of the railroad to Pine Point. Of course, this is something which had been projected for some time, and it was only when the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company were prepared to go ahead and develop a vast lead and zinc project at Pine Point it became practicable to build the railway, and I give the administration full marks for having carried out that plan. After all, in the five years they have been in power we are surely entitled to expect some measure of development.
With respect to the Pine Point project and the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company development I believe the hon. member estimated that the expenditures would be in the neighbourhood of some $28 million, having regard to the developments at Trail and at Pine Point itself. The national energy board, is at the present time reviewing the application of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company for a power interconnection with the Bonneville Power Corporation. If this project is agreed to by the national energy board, it will mean a projected development in the city of Kimberley alone of some $85 million.
Mr. Chairman, with the short time at my disposal, obviously I cannot get through the major part of my address. I hope this debate continues, but in the meantime I believe, because of the urgency of the situation with respect to the unemployment insurance fund, I should bring this matter to the attention of the administration, if it has not already been done so a sufficient number of times. According to the advisory council of the unemployment insurance commission, we are facing a complete bankruptcy of the fund. I have from time to time asked the Minister of Labour what he proposes to do about it, but of course he does not appear to worry. It is approaching winter very rapidly, but we are told that some time this fall we are going to have the report of the Gill committee, which I believe was set up some time last year. This report of the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission is a document of despair. In at least three places in this document there is the plea that the government should do something to strengthen the fund. The committee points out that at the end of May, 1962 there was only $20 million in the fund, and that by September it would probably reach a maximum of $70 million. If that were so it would be necessary, in order to make the fund solvent for

Ways and Means
the full year to provide approximately another $74 million; that is, as a direct grant from the government. But, of course, they recommend against grants, except on occasion to bring the fund into solvency immediately. The actual figures for the build-up throughout the summer amount to some $75 million, where something in the neighbourhood of $70 million was projected.
So that we are in this unhappy position in respect of an insurance fund which some five years ago stood at close to $1 billion- $928 million, if my memory serves me correctly. Throughout the five years of Conservative administration, while they have not done nothing-they have increased the rates, and I believe they also took into the fund those of a higher income category-this Conservative administration has taken no action to revise the whole program so that the fund would become solvent again. They have said throughout these years that there has been full employment, that there has been no real unemployment situation; yet throughout these same five years the fund has been depleted.
Somewhere along the line somebody is not being truthful. If the fund was solvent in 1956 and we had full employment, or near full employment at that time, and this has continued, why has the fund depreciated by almost $1 billion?

Tomorrow will be legislation, Mr. Speaker. First the resolution in the name of the Minister of Agriculture dealing with the Farm Credit Act, item No. 27 on today's order paper. The second item will be Bill No. C-3, to amend the Food and Drugs Act, which is item No. 2 on today's order paper. And if we have time, the third item will be Bill No. C-4, to amend the Department of National Health and Welfare Act, No. 3 on today's order paper.
